" Gallant Little Wales."—Tae Welsh Industries Sale and Exhibiticn, held last week at the Albert Hall in London, when many notable representatives of promi- nent Welsh families had charge of or assisted at the stalls, proved a great success. The famons Welsh bomeepun—egaiust which the only complaint that can be brought is that it positively refuses to wear out— went off briskly •, so also did the beautiful embroideries and pottery. A feature of the Sale was a huge pyramid of Welsh dolls which disappeared in an incredibly short epee° of time. The Oldest Doll in the World,—Apropas of dolls, one supposed to be the oldest in the world is of Emden origin, stud now in the collection of al r.Edmund 'Lovett. It is said to have been made WO B.C. The opinion of sunny people seems to le that little girls- now-a-days care corsidc•rably less for dolls than did our grand- mothers in the days of their youth, but bearing in mind the vast numbers of dolls that come into the markets, and are sold enneally, this notice is not likely to be , correct. PessiLly, however, girls give up dolls at an earlier age than formerly, which after ell is not an item 1 greatly to deplore. • The Irish Leader's Daughters--Miss Johanna Redmond, whose little play "Leap Year in the West," was pro- duced at a London theatre last week, is the younger daughter of 31e. John Redmond, the leader of the Irish Nationalist Party. The play deals with an , incident of life in the West of Ireland, and shows the efforts of a girl to make her bashful lover understand how much she is devoted to him. This part was taken I by her elder sister Miss Esther Redmond, who is to be I married in London neat week to Dr. W. T. Power, of 1. New York. Miss Johanna Redmond is only twenty ; years of age. but she has written several stories, which 1 have been published, and her elder sister shares her' literary end artistic tastes. 'Mr. Balfour at Sixty.—Mr. Arthur J. Balfour will be sixty on the flath ef this month, and as the saOrrs go on I the prospect of his joing the earls of the Beneclicts appears to aecorre more and more remote. Society 1 matrons will have to regard him as one of the conflrmed bachelors. hut fore long time they were loth to do so. Mr. Balfour was one of those who long enjoyed the reputation of being a young roan. There are msny distinguished men in public life who are never regarded otherwise, until well past middle age. Mr. Joseph Chamberlain was one of there, noel it was not generally] realised that ho was getting on in yeers, until his health . broke down, when he was on the threshold of the allotted span of three score years and ten. Similarly it will come almost as a shock to many people to learn • that Mr. Balfour has left the fifties behind. it is I different•with widowers, het that is a time of life at I which hem a mat rirroninl point of view, the bachelor I beCOMES rather a hopelers rpecular. Dress at Ilenley.—Henley of course is a boy and girl 1 fete primarily, ore looks there for simple fashions, and this year certainly found them. The girls who aimed 1 at leaig useful was °imbed in linen of the soft uncrush- able order, printed' cotton, chintz, or firm zephyr, and instead of the frilly baby hat which really snits only the very few, even among the prettiest and freshest faces, the sun bonnet was widely chosen. This is an ideal covering for river wear, as it not only protects the face but the back of the 'neek also. In printed cottons and cleiatzee, the son-bonnet is especially charm- ing, especially when worn with a dainty little white lawn cap inside, and IJCSB flowing strings. The girl -vile elected to be orrnmental ouly, evidently preferred white muslin of the limp order, with just a touch of colour short the waistlelt nod in the hat, the sunshade repeating the hue of course. White muslin is in great request for evening wear for quite young girls, when it is mounted over soft, ivory Oriental satin, Loth the muslin and sip appearing, as is desired at the moment, so limp as to give the impression of having been drawn through water before wearina. • The Extra Length of "Materiel.—There is little chance of our summer frocks being peered away in tissue paper this reneindeed many of es are overlooking anxiously our airy-fairy mnslins and cool linens, and wondering nhether they will last out the season, so hard have we worn them. Garden parties are the order of the day, and although pretty gowns look charming sweeping the velvety lawns, such a procedure is certainly tad for the hems and firmness, that "sweep." And this fact affords yet another example of the inestimable nsefulness of the extra yard or two of materiel lying in wait to be called into service for repairs. When purchasing a dress length we should never forget this extra piece which bestows upon so manygovrns a further sphere of usefelness. Flowers for Mts.—Early in the season flowers were 'mixed upon modish headgear, as many as seven or eight kinds frequently appearing upon one " creation." But we have changed all that, now only ore kind of bloom is used—roses for choice. At the sales 'many a 'spray of roses can be piched up cheapely,and we should do well to seize upon snch bargains, as e haterer flowers are in or out of fashion, roses remain. All the ladies of our floyal Family shew a preference this summer for roses, especially those of natural bee. aIADGE.

SUN-BONNETS AND HATS.

The return of the sun-bonnet is a welcome re- vival. On very young girls nothing, says a Globe writer', could be more charming than this old-fashioned headgear. In flowered prints it is, of course, most correct; but in printed cottons and chintzes, and even in old-fashioned muslins, it is very pretty with ribbon strings. Some girls put ddinty little caps of white lawn inside, lightly resting on the hair. This is a very suc- cessful coquetry. The sun-bonnet has much to recommend it, particularly the curtain at the back, which protects the neck from sunburn; but those who have quantities of pretty hair do not affect it. Frilly sun-hats do not hide the hair nearly so much, but they are far from being universally becoming. They suit frivolous pretti- ness, or gay beauty; but above, a thou,ghtful type of face, however young, they appear incon- gruous. There is one kind of river-hat which ought to be suppressed—the elaborate kind. This pretends to follow the simple-Susie lines of the real thing, but it is .wired and curved and frilled out of knowledge—or made 'of fine Mechlin lace, or of painted chiffon—the beauty that perisheth. Moreover, it is trimmed with velvet and gold flowers, or silver or gold ribbons. or other such sophisticated garnitures. It is set on a bandeau, and is obviously meant to be worn on an elaborate arrangement of puffs and curls. These hats are anomalies. The miss the beauties of both town and country.. • SKInT.

Pictured in, our illustration is a smart and useful skirt which has been specially designed with a view to its realisation in Shantung or linen. Shantung is extraordinarily fashionable this summer, and as it wears spHulidly, and washes- like the proverbial rag, it is an excellent investment as a dressy odd skirt to wear with a prettjr muslin or lawn blouse for tennis or

garden parties, or similar summer festiriiics. The particular model pictured in our sketch is quite simple in shape, being merely a box- pleated affait, with all the pleao, which are wide, firmly machined for some little distance below the waist, thus forming a sheath-like top to the skirt. This is an easy model for the amateur to attempt, and is wonderfully effective and becoming. A FASCINATING MOTOR - BONNET.

The motor-car is responsible for the revival of another old fashion, that of the close-fitting straw bonnet. It is not tho coal-scuttle nor the scoop-brimmed headgear that we called Early Victorian, writes. Clare North in 31.A.1'., but a bonnet that frames tho face without projecting over it. It is trimmed with ribbon put on sedately, or perhaps with. gauza and a few flowers that resist sun, dust, and wind as well as may be. Over this headgear a veil of gauze to match tho trimming is worn, and anything more fascinating or becoming to a pretty girl it is hardly possible to imagine. TO-DAY'S ItECIPE.

div.p: INOMEWS GHAT.
SCIENCE NOTES AND NEWS.

OIL AND AMMONIA FROM SEWAGE. In a paper read by Mr. F. Purcell before the Institution of Mining Engineers a new method of sewage utilisation is described. The solid matter, known as "sludge," is dis- tilled in a similar manner to that adopted for oil -shale. The product is gas, crude oil, and ammonium sulphate. From the residue cement is manufactured. The gas is used in drying the sludge. _ From one ton of sludge from nine to ton gallons of oil, and from 571 b. to 651 b.—and. even 1001 b.—of ammo- nium sulphate have been obtained. This method of utilising sewage promises to be a profitable way of disposing of it.

THE OUTER AND INNER PLANETS. The phases and apparent diameters a Mercury, Venus, and - Mars are subject to great variations during their revolution around the sun • but owing to their greater distances from the earth, tne, changes in the apparent diameters of Jupiter and Saturn are not so marked; while those of Uranus and Neptune are barely perceptible. The brilliance of a planet depends upon its Mag- nitude ; its distance from the sun; its dis- tance from the earth; and the extent of the illuminated area which is visible from our planet. On account of their great distance from the earth, the major planets always shew their illuminated surfaces; therefore the phases are confined to the terrestrial planets.

div.head: TO DESTROY MOSQUITOES.
div.p: TO DESTROY MOSQUITOES.

The plan of spreading a thin layer of retroleum over the surface of ponds, Sze., where mosquitoes spend the larval stage of their existence has been found effectual. In hot climates, however, the petroleum evapo- rates too quickly. Experiments carried out at Gaboon, in French Africa, shew that in tropical regions cactus paste is a more effec- tive substance. To make it the thick pulpy leaves of the cactus are cut in pieces and macerated in water. This forms • a sticky paste, which is spread on the surface of the stagnant waters. Not being able to come to the surface to breathe, the mosquito larvso perish. The larva) period lasts only two weeks, while the layer of cactus pulp remains effective for months,

div.head: GROWTH OF MAN.
div.p: THE GROWTH OF MAN.

Observations regarding the growth of man have determined the following interesting facts: The most rapid growth takes place im- mediately after birth, the growth of an in- fant during the first year of its existence being about Sin. The ratio of increase gra-. dually decreases until the age of three. years is reached, at which time the size attained is about half that which it is to become when full grown. After five years the succeeding increase is very regular until the sixteenth, being at the ,rate for the average man of 2in. a-year. Beyond sixteen the growth is feeble, being for the following two years about six- tenths of an inch a-year, while from eighteen to twenty the increase in height is seldom over an inch. At the age of twenty-five the growth ceases, save in a few exceptional cases.

div.head: TO DETECT IMITATION HONEY.
div.p: TO DETECT IMITATION HONEY.

Imitation honey is made by several pro- cesses. The commonest consists in boiling a thick syrup of sugar mixed with a very small proportion of mineral -acid. The sugar is thus converted into invert sugar, or a mix- ture of dextrose and levulose, similar to the sugar of natural honey. By mixing this imita- tion honey with natural honey of strong flavour, a product is obtained which deceives the best judges of honey. The fraud can be .detected, however, by means of Ley's re- agent, which is prepared in the following manner: Ten parts of silver nitrate, dis- solved in 100 parts of water, are mixed with 20 parts of a 15 per cent. solution of sodium carbonate. The precipitate which falls is re- moved by filtration, washed, and dissolved in 115 parts of a 10 per cent. solution of ammo- nium chloride. The solution is kept in well. stoppered bottles in the. dark. A few drops of this solution are added to a little of the suspected honey, diluted with twice its weight of water, and the mixture is heated for five minutes on a water bath in the dark. In these conditions natural honey turns dark brown and exhibits greenish-yellow fluorescence; while imitation honey assumes a lighter brown tint and shews no fluorescence. It is asserted that the presence of as- small a pro- portion of imitation honey as 25- per cent. cnn be detected in this way.

div.head: COAL FROM' THE DUST-BIN.
div.p: COAL FROM' THE DUST-BIN.

tinder the title of Coalesine, Mr. H. G. Coales describes in the Engineering Review a new fad which may be made from the re- fuse of the dust-bin. 'ln its manufacture the double purpose of removing a nuisance, and forming a useful product is achieved. To make cealesine the contents of the dust-bin are first pulverised by a machine known as a dust manipulator. Its 501 b. hammers make 1,000 revolutions in a minute, and reduce the refuse to a powder resembling garden mould. This has a distinct value as a fer- tiliser i for any reason- its further manipula- tion is undesirable. The dust is then mixed with certain tar compounds, and pressed into briquettes, which are then ready for use as fuel. The tar serves three purposes, it deo- dorises the refuse, aeglutinates the duet, and enriches the fuel. It is found to increase the calorific value cf poor refuse 100 per cent., and of good 50 per cent. The cost of maliing 10,000 tons of coalesine is found to be or 4s. a ten. In heating Power slb. of coalesine are equivalent to , lib. of the best coal. Thus an outlay of I2s, in eoalesine will give the heating power of a ton of thc•best coal.

div.head: WHY MOTHS LIKE THE FLAME.
div.p: WHY MOTHS LIKE THE FLAME.

The mysteries of the moth And the flame have been solved. The moth, like many other insects, flies to the flame for the same reason that the sunflower and other plants turn to the light. Heliotropism is the awesome name in which this tendency of plants and animals . rejoices. Insects move in the direction of the light rays that fall upon them. Change the posi- tion of the light and the insect changes -his position. Expose the insect to a diffused •light, and it will move towards the bright- ness with measured pace and slow, but ex. pose him to a brilliant glare and he hastens with cheerful alacrity. That is Why - winged insects flutter gaily about in the direct sun- light. Heliotropism actually aids an insect in its struggle for existence. Certain caterpillars, just after they pre hatched, and when they are ravenously hun- gry, are compelled by the mechanical effect of light to crawl to the tips of the branches, where they End their first nourishment in tender buds. After their first meal the cater- pillars lose much of their sensitiveness to light. Their heliotropism explains much that has been attributed vaguely to instinct.

div.head: WHAT MAKES HAILSTONES.
div.p: WHAT MAKES HAILSTONES.

The formation of hail through electrical action, according to the new theory of scien- tists attached to the Weather Bureau at Washington, is an interesting and even won- derful process. The wind draws out a cloud into a long, narrow strip. In that form, owing to the great amount of surface ex- posed to the air, the cloud evaporates rapidly, and the rapid evaporation produces intense cold.. Dry particles of• snow are then formed, and these, by friction with the water drops, quickly become charged with nega- tive electricity. But the water drops them- sAves carry positive electricity, and, since negative attracts positive, a film of water is formed upon each snow particle, and is in- stantly frozen into a layer of ide. At this thickness its outer, surface remains moist, the water not freezing there so rapidly, whereupon the electrical charge changes from negative to positive, and the particle is re- pelled by the water drops and dtiven to the outer parts of the cloud. Here the increased cold covers it with snow agrin, and friction charges it anew with negative electricity. Re- pulsion is now once more changed for attrao- tion, and the particles rush back into the cloud, receiving upon their surfaces another film of water, which is turned into second ice I layers. Thus the growing hailstone darts zig- zag cnrougn tne clouds, piling up its alter- nate layers of snow and ice until gravitation gains control, and sends it, with a jingling crowd of its fellows, spinning to the grouncl.

There paragraphs will have no interest for thore uho are alieady photographers, and it is only some three months 'since I had a set of notes nrsing non-photo- graphers to take up camera work. Still, there are so many people just tempted into the camera habit by the sunshine and the holidays, that I give up mt 'column again to their interests. WHO OUGHT TO PHOTOGIIAPH.

Perhaps the simpler question would be, who ought not to photograph, and the answer would be, the man who has absolutely no spare titre or spare money he is to be pitied. Every one vho Las time for a hobby and even a very few shillings to spend upon it, should let that' hobby be photography, or should add photo- graphy to his existing hobbies. I will say no more on this head.

. COW'S REMATUCABLE MILIC YIELD.

A shorthorn cow at the Royal Show in Newcastle yielded an exceptionally large quantity of milk. At the morning milking she gave 411 b. l4oz, of milk, and at the evening milking 361 b. 140 z., or 781 b. for the day. At home the yielded to pounds more. This is said to be a record. The cow was Lord Rothschild's Darling- ton Cranford ; she was born October 26, 1897, xnd calved ou April 9, 1908.

question was, how could she get out of the bed- room, when Elsbeth was positive she had bolted . the door, and the window was iron-barred? "It's uncanny, that it is! " Elsbeth moaned, 1 clasping and unclasping her big, sinewy hands. The inspector walked rdund Delicia's 'room, 1 tapping the panelling. Then he gave a low, I pleased whistle. - A fragment of dress material, between two of the panels, caught his observant eye. He inserted the strong blade of a penknife, and the panel opened slowly inwards, revealing the landing and staircase. The inspector showed the scrap of brown cloth to Elsbeth. "Seen this before ? " She took it and held it close to her small, crafty eyes. " It's like the frock Miss Delicia wears." "That's the way she escaped, then. We must find Miss Delicia.' They found her at the Vicarage. Miss Mere- dith told how she was awakened at two o'clock by gravel being thrown against her window. and, looking out, she saw Delicia. The girl seemed greatly excited and troubled, saying she would never return to her. uncle, and imploring Miss Meredith to shelter her. When told of her uncle's death, Delicia appeared like one stunned —she did not cry, but looked, and looked, with wide, dark eyes, which held a hidden terror in their depths. Truly, for Barrington that was a day of startling events, which reached their climax with the arrest of Delicia, charged with the murder of her uncle. At first she seemed about to offer vehement protests, then relapsed into a stony silence, from which nothing aroused her until Austen was granted periglesion for an in- terview. "Delicia, my darling, this is all a ghastly mis- take. What are they thinking about? Trust me, dearest;; you shall won be a free woman." "No, the law must take its course," Delicia answered, quietly. "I am prepared to take my trial, and am not afraid of the result. But you and I must never meet again." "Why, Delicia? But you are upset. You do not know what you say. Alt, my darling, it breaks my heart to see you suffer. "Oh, I am brave—l will be brave," she told him, her eyes shining with a strange brilliancy. Time was up. With lagging footsteps, Austen turned away, leaving Delicia alone in the cell— alone with her thoughts. At the coroner's in- quest, the jury returned a verdict of murder against Delieia, and the case would go for trial to the next assizes, six weeks hence. The chief witness was Elsbeth; she 'told •of the quarrel be- tween the old man and Delicia, and the previous quarrel with Austen Rivers. When she men- tioned this, Delicia grasped the rail in front of her, swaying for a moment, then pulled herself together with an effort. But she kept her eyes resolutely turned away from Austen, and would not meet the passionate gaze he fixed so intently on her face. During the days which followed he was almost distraught with grief. His practice, everything might go. What did anything matter but the awful fact that Delicia was in prison on fake charge? r • AtlBioll was prepared to devote every farthing he possessed to secure Deficia's acquittal. Josephs, K.C., famous for his success in criminal cases, was . briefed for the! defence, and the Mullhampton 'Assize Court was crowded on the day of the trial. A little thrill went through the spectators as Dolicia took her place , in the dock, the only prisoner awaiting trial on the capital chate. With a face as white as death, her eyes looked more startlingly, large and dark in contrast. For one swift second she raised them to where Austen eat, then stood gaz- ing straight before her—a still, slim figure, pathetically young and girlish-looking. The prosecution laid stress on the fact of the quarrel of Simon . being the barrier between Delicia and her lover, which would supply a v for the murder Apparently he had been motive attacked in his 'sleep, and, being old and feeble, it would take no more than the girl's strength to choke tle breath out of him. In answer to a question, Elsbeth replied that it would be easy for anyone to force the kitchen window from the ! outside, and gain an entrance to the, house. She- repeated what Austen had said to that effect, and stated that, as she slept in an attic at the top of the house, she could not easily hear what went on downstairs. It had been Mr. Hols- worth's custom to sit up after she and Miss Delicia retired. Sometimes he would spend the night in his chair by the fire. No, burglary could not !Jaye been the motive since Mr. Hols- worth's valuable watch and chain were untouched. Then Mr. Josephe rose, hitched up his gown, and began his speech for the defence. He took up the line that all the evidence was purely cir- oumstantial, and Mr. Holsworth being a man of eccentric habits, reported a miser, what more likely than that the crime was committed by a burglar? Probably he was startleclain some way, and so made off without securing any booty. Date the jary upon such slight evidence, which had to be filled in and pieced together by his learned brother, condemn the girl, whose affec- tion for her uncle was well known? , When counsel wound up his impassioned ad- dress, which laded an hour and a quarter, there was some applause, which was speedily sup- pressed. Then came the Judge's summing-up, the careful sifting of 'the evidence, the judic;al impartiality with which he weighed every' point for and against. , When the twelve good men and true retired to consider their verdict, Delicia was conducted below. Twenty minutes, thirty passed. Once more she took her place in the dock, feeling as one in a dream— the stalwart warders, the 1 policemen, the little be-robed, be-wigged man on the bench, the close, gas-lit atmosphere, the sea of faces, all were part of this strange dream. It was only the sight of Austen, with his eyes full of love, pity, and longing fixed upon her, I which recalled Delicia to the reality of the I scene. The silence was so deep that the pro- verbial pin-drop could have been heard when 1 the foremanof the jury returned a verdict of • "Not Guilty?" "Thank heaven'!" Austen leant forward and , covered his face with his heads. Ile felt a curious sensation of exhaustion now that the suspense was over. Delicia leant heavily on the rail, her breath coming in &hog, quick gasps, then she fell to the ground' in a dead faint. I s

Delicia was safely settled at the vicarage with the Merediths (who had never once doubted her innocence) when the news came that Austen Rivers was arrested on the cilarge for which, Delicia had stood her trial. The kinly old Vicar broke the terrible tidings to Delicia. " Thc+t police are getting in a muddle over the affair," ho said. • They will be arresting me next. div.p: SAVING THE BABIES. Splendid Success of Sir John Brunner's Bonus Scheme.

Sir John Brunner's generous scheme to save the babies of Winnington is referred to in the report of the Northwicla and Mid-Cheshire branch of the I.‘,T.S.P.C.C. At the beginning of 190(3 Sir John Brunner promised —in emulation of Alderman Broadbent, of Huddersfield —to give £1 to he parents of every child, born in Winnington, providing the child reached the age of twelve months, and was reported to be healthy and well cared for. .

Each birth had to be reported to a special registrar. On receipt of the notification infc,rwation is sent to the district nurse, along with a supervision paper and a leaflet on" How to bring up a baby." The nurse visits. all through the twelve months, and reports on the birth- day upon the condition of the child. Sixteen children were registered in 1906 and twenty-- four in 1067. Up to April, 1968, £23 had been paid, and not a single registered child has died. For the five years ending 1905, the mortality of infants in Winnington was 121 undcr one year per 1,000 born ; for the two years 1909 and 1907 it was 7/5. The registra- tion for the bonus "scheme is voluntary, and not all the children that .re born are registered. The report added : "lii considering the value of any schemes for reducing infantile mortality that involve continuous supervision of the children, it must not be forgotten that the net gain to the nation is not merely that many lives are saved, but that many who would- possibly have reached the age of twelve months probably become stronger for the cam o bestowed upon them. increasing the chance of their living to a greater age."

The train had pulled up at a tiny country station of the "five miles from anywhere" type, and it was raining in torrents; the hour between, eleven and twelve, with a bitterly cold north- east wind blowing. Tho station was in darkness, and closed; the last train timed to stop had gone -two hours ago; and the combination official— Porter and stationmaster in one—had departed. All the passengers in this. train, save two, had alighted at previous stations. These two were a gentleman and lady who occupied a first-class compartment: the former a tall, good-looking, deeply-bronzed man of about five-and-thirty, wrapped in a,richly-furred overcoat; the latter a slender girl of perhaps twenty, with fair, fluffy hair and beautiful dark-grey eyes. She was dressed in mourning„, very simply, but there was no appearance of poverty about her. She did not belong to-her travelling companion, but had got in some fifty nibs higher up the line, and they had got into conversation, and were beguiling the time quite pleasantly when the train came to a deadstop at a station where it was not timed to stop at all. The destination of both was fifty miles beyond this place.
. . •" Whew-w t" said the gentleman: "what's to le done? What place is this, guard?" " Little Bellingham, air." "A village?" " That's all; three ndles from the station, air."

"And no house of any sort nearer?" "Ne'er a one, sir—not even a cottage." "Well, this is a fix," said the gentleman to his oornpanion. "I shouldn't mind for myself, I've knocked about too much. and I'm a .man; but •for a lady it's avvkwaid. We must •get out, anyhow." "Train'll be shunted on to a siding—'bout a up,s sir," said the guard. "Where it would ,be delightfully cold -in this confounded nor' easter. We must manage something better than that. Have you any lug- gage?" to his companion. Ho took down a evaliee from the rack as he spoke. No--noth in g," she said. 'e -about me--I am not dismayed." "You are a brave girl not to be; but I'm going to find out if there's any place of shelter open befere that train runs out. A coach would be better than this platform. Luckily, rye got --a light." He produced from the pocket of his overcoat a reading-lamp, and proceeded to make an jasper- lion. 'All right!" he exclaimed, after finding -the booking-office and porter's room locked up; "here's a tiny waiting-room open." The train by this time had begun to move . backwards. The guard called out "Good-night, 'sir," and the lights flashed away into th-o dark- ness. The, two travellers were alone. "Look here," the man said. "I'll do what I s can to make you comfortable. If you don't mind being in the dark for a little while I'll try and manage a fire. It will be jolly cold for you without °ilea You see, I don't know how. I could find my way to the village, and probably couldn't raise a trap there, anyway: besides, this a lonesome place to leave you all that time -by yourself." "Indeed!" she said, "I should be afreid: be. "Bides, I wouldn't have you go out in such a storm on my account!" "Oh! the storm-'—that is nothing. By-the bye," he added, with a bright laugh, that was in itself a guarantee, "perhaps it might he handier if you knew my name—Guise, Maurice Guise, just home from South Africa." "Thank you," said the girl, smiling. "It is 'more convenient to know names—under such eir, camstances as these. My. name is Verner." "Thank you. Now to try and get some feel." "Can't I help you?" "What! 'Come out in the rain? No. Vole sit down, please, and I'll do that work." The girl 'obeyed, laughingly. The adventure eppealed to 'her sense of fun, and she felt perfect faith in her aompanion. 'He had the ease and freedom from conventionality of the Colonial and citizen of the world, with the chivalry and courtesy of the -gentleman, "to the manner born." She was some little time alone; then the light • gleamed ,again, and Maurice • Guise aepeared, atriumphant. "Look here!" said he, "corn as g.vl3t—l found this old crate up in a corner. ..a.nd. I commandeered coals from a heap by ,the "n9"-this ne.wspaper—lucky I bought one— _ flislies the lot " "How lovely! Can you light a fire?" • "You'll see. Miss Verner, if I can." Ile proved himself an expert. The wood was a little damp. but. Guise used it freely, and - and-bye there was a merry little fire in the . .grate. "Now," said he, when the fire had burnt up, "I'll fetch- some more coals, to fix you up fcr :the night. He went away, and presently came back with a luggage truck which he had dis- covered; over the truck was a piece of sacking, and a goodly quantity of coals on the saeltiaa. "I'll make it good to the company," he said, laughing-, as lie and Marjorie Verner carried the !acking between them into the waiting-room. 'NOW, Miss Verner.' as to commiaiariat, rye Rot a flask of brandy and some biscuits—nothing -else, I am sorry to say; but they are at your a service." will have some biscuits, if you will," she 'aid quickly. "No brandy, thanks—not now, • any rate." You may need. it by-and-bye." he said, kin,.dlv "and as to the biscuits—l've gone with- • out food for thirty hours before now, and been - none the worse for it in the end." . "All the same," slie `said.' "I shall not touch 2 "lam unless you take your share. I am not Thado of blown glass, you know." :`Maybe•not," said Guise, "but a ania should more care for a woman, shouldn't he? than •. Perhaps she takes for herself. I hate to see a naarnan suffer—and they're always wanting to Rive up things I" "Well, you are doing that now," said !! Marjorie. -Ii into laughed, and put a few biscuits his 'Pocket. "I'm afraid you'll not get much sleep s noise of 'these chairs," be said. , 'I am not a bit sleepy," .Marjorie answered. 4 s; I make nothing of sitting up all night. I have caone it many a time: but if you can manage a 'lO2O, Mr. 'Guise, I shan't be offended." e a ea, I? he said, surprised. "I am going out- • . "No, indeed!" interrupted Marjorie. a‘a In the cold—it's perishing in that wind." a. "Oh! I'm all right with this coat, and I'can valk up and down if I'm cold. Good-night, Miss verner." • "Mr. Guise--I couldn't think of it. I couldn't ,sait down by this fire, and you. who have been no :kind, freezing out there. We are coreratics in -amisfortune, aren't we? and ehouid share and "'hare alike." Guise yielded. It was the riglit thing—the MY thing—for him to do. The circumstances ~.les..roke down ordinary conventions: they were "KG People cast upon a desert island: and under such conditions men and women, who, perhaps. saaly met for the first time a few hours before feel as if they had known each other for years. . Guise sat down on one side of the fire, Mar- ie on the other. They at the biscuits, and `ney talked, while the rain beat upon the statiori :ealeal, and the wind howled and shrieked round e rickety little structure. Maurice Guise :si.Vaved himself a most entertaining companion. r a had had all sorts -of adventures. seen many - ands and peoples, and always used his eyes; he, on his side, thought he had never met a Possessing greater charm, combined with a. , ,f aight intelligence. than Marjorie Veruer. He —414 Positively giateful to the flood which had •rown them together like this, though it saorned selfish to feel so. There was no noneense about this girl—no blushing and timidity, and a9bvious consciousness of being in an embarrass. 'A:l,g Position. She accepted it simply, gracefully. " aanawing with whom she had to deal, putting. her .WMPanlOl.l at his en. Fir because she, herself was embarrassed. Guise found himself flanking at those dark grey eyes had a wonderful (arc- for expressing deep emotion, and that a man • Ott do many things to make them look or eirk,:! with favour. "I hope," he said once witl"at YOU are not anxious about any friend, , 'ha s. May be worrying on your account. We shel . • able to telegraph in the morning, I daresay. tiro ‘a'se the wires are blown down." qflariorie shook her head. "No.', she said , T don't think they will worry much, thanks!" he ve , must be strange people, then, ho salt utillreSelf, to be indifferent about such a girl perhaps her present destination was not 'vjetrigs•l "I wonder," he said, after a pause, 3'ou know some people at Canmore to whom going. In fact "—he lauahed—" I am sup. •Dep.e.„(l to be half engaged to the daughter; bus eea nv away only these beenseven months ri or s at Canmoe," I.arlor hie said; "but I might know the people." 0910'Ne1t0n is the name—" She started, and used slightly. 1 "Mrs. Norton—living at the Cedars?" "Yes," he said, half eagerly. "I am nursery governess to the two little girls," said Marjorie, quietly. . " Are you?" exclaimed Guise, in a' pleased tone. "Why,. then, I shall have the pleasure of meeting you there." "I don't think so. My- sphere is the nursery. 'Governess' is a euphemism; the children Ore very young—only six and four." , "But, surely—" Guise began, drawing his brows together; he paused, and bit his lip. i Then he added, "A lady is a lady, Surely they treat you as one, Miss Verner?" "Oh, yes! I don't mix with the servants; but ' I don't expect to be in the drawing-room. That would be absurd; one must accept a position on its merits." . . "Philosophically—yes; but philosophy is some- times a hard pill to swallow. You haven't heard them, then, speak of me?" "No; I scarcely see them, and Miss Norton has been away some weeks; she only came home a few days ago." . .Guise was silent. He had been promising him- self the pleasure of escorting his companion to her destination; but perhaps he could hardly do that under the circumstances; it would be a- " cruel kindness," and .might provoke questions hard to answer. .He presently turned to discuss- ing ways of reaching Canmore, and found that by driving some miles •across country another line could be reached. "In that caso," ho said, "I shall have the pleasure of driving you across to the junction, and seeing you into the Can- more train." And Marjorie understood and ap- preciated the delicacy which prevented his pro- posing .to accompany her the whole distance. . The dawn broke at last; the rain had ceased ;it was now possible to take steps towards getting away; and at last, after considerable difficulty, , Guise managed to get himself and Marjorie : driven over to Ledbury Junction in a carrier's ! cart. They stopped at an inn on the road, and • had some much-needed breakfast, and then went on their way rejoicing. And in the early after- noon Marjorie Verner reached the Cedars. 1..... . . . . "lie seems to have come home as poor as he went out." Marjorie heard these words from Mrs. Norton's lips, as she came to fetch the two little girls to bed. Guise, she' knew, had not ' long arrived. She herself had eeplained her Inon-appearance, telling the trouble, and only suppressing that part which referred to her com- panion. Guise was now changing his travelling ' dress, and Mrs. Norton . and her stepdaughter— Ella was the child of' a former marriage—were sitting in the drawing-room, evidently discussing the new arrival. Ella was a handsome young woman of twenty-five, for whetri . Marjorie had no particular liking—so far as she had seen Miss Norton. , . , .. "Yes" Ella answered; "I wonder what he can have been doing all these years? How came he by that coat? The fur is sable." "I daresay that is a gift ; he certainly could not have bought it. From what he said, I gather he has no assured income. Run away to bed, children; you as& keeping Miss Verner waiting." Marjorie led the little ones away, and heard no more of the conversation; but it struck her that Ella Norton hardly looked like a girl whose lover had returned to her after an absence of seven years. She seemed something more than i annoyed that he had come back empty-handed. ' A day or two later she came face to face with ' Maurice Guise in one ,of the corridors. He give a quick look round,. and held out his • hand. "Well met, Miss Verner," he said. "I am so pleased to see you again. You got back without any further mishap, I hope?" "Oh, yet, thanks L" - " That's right. I am beginning to learn my lesson." • . "Your lesson? "—with an inquiring look. "Ares," he said, gravely; "the differentia be- tween what one is and what one has." " Ah!. That is an old story," said Marjosie, • smiling. "You would expect that, wouldn't you?" ' "Oh, yes, I am not surprised; and then. I . ought to have made a fortune and I, didn't I make it, and I'm afraid- that is an unpardonable I crime. You want to be off? Well, good-bye, for : the present. I trust we shall meet again soon." 1 So 'did lislarjorie—mentally. She half sighed as she passed on. She felt sorry fcr the man; , and yet she did not fancy—from what he said I last night, and just now, and his manner—that his own affections had been deeply engaged with Ella Norton. Only it might be a matter of honour. , It chanced—or it seemed to chance-'—that two I or three times after this Maurice Guise came across Marjorie when she was 'walking in the grounds with her charges. She was happy enough to be with him, and hardly knew how to avoid such meetings; to tell him he must merely bow or shako hands when they suet and pass on, would seem like giving too much point to the meetings:- and she had not the will .to shut these hours of sunshine out, of her life., But one day she summoned resolution, and gave him , a hint. " I wonder," she said, "that on such a lovely afternoon, you are not riding or driving with Miss Norton.'" He , shook his head and laughed. "Miss Nor- ton - can dispense with my society," he said, "without beeaking her heart—or mine either, • for that matter." . " Because you are poor?" "Because I am poor. That's natural enough, ' isn't it?" "Why, yes—" • , "They asked rae for 'at least three weeks,' and I am taking them at their word. Oh! they don't give me hints to go—they arc too well bred for that; anal Ella likes to 'have a cavalier in attendance sometimes ; but she snakes mo understand—as women can—that I must not pass beyond a certain line. I don't want to do so—that's one thing." , Marjorie wsls , silent. The corollary was ir- , resistible, that if Maurice Guise stayed in a house where he wasn't particularly wanted, and did not stay for Ella's sake, he -staVed for her (Marjorie's) sake. He certainly sought her; and his Manner, the tones of his voice, often made her heart beat faster. She could not think he was only amusing himself;, was he, than, just letting himself drift—or was it more than that? Already more than a fortnight of the three weeks had gone. Guise :could not exceed the tinia without invitation, and that invitation it did not appear he was likelY to get. To-day, when he parted from the girl—which he always dm before they were near the house—he 'said, "Don't you ever steull out in the evening?" i " Sometimes," she said, a little Startled, "on I the terrace." I 1 " Well "—he had her hand in his,. and teemed ; to have forgotten to drop it—" you might ex- I tend your walk this evening—to the shrubbery. ' Will you?" Marjorie flushed crimson; her eyes sank; her btcath came quickly; the 193 S silent. " You know," said Guise, softly, "I. can't talk to you—with these children about. You must hi good to me—and come. When are you free?" , , "At eight o'clock." "Thanks. Tl:en—au revoir." His clasp tightened fcr u inm,:sut ; then he turned away and left her. and Marjorie walked back to. the house, in a hind of dream.' She had promised to 'elect Maurice Guise; she could not g:'., back on her word if she ac;uld ; she would not if she could. ,

Frain the black shadow of the trees a tall fujo st.iiried out; Marjotie'i trembling hands vere drawn into a warin Clasp, and covered with ec•ft kisses. " Forgive Inc ! " Maurice Guisa whispered; "forgive me! You know I love you, Marjorie; and you care for rite a little, don't you?"

7.; "Net a little !"—she answered, very low; "with all my heart!" Then his arms were about her; her head pil- lowed on his brecst, his lips on hr;a; and, for many r4r-ites silence. Then Guiee - said, ten- dorly, You arc not afraid of poverty, Marjorie?"
"Oh, no! rio ! " "[f I asked you to wrjt for me until I could make a home for my wife, you would wait?" "For years."

" Tho "saine brave, pure spirit that drew mine to you that night in the little station," said Guise, softly. ," Well, there will be no., need for that, darling. I have. enough for comfort, if not luxury. So we -need not Fait."

They strolled uri •and down in paradi.se, con- scions only of each othc.r, till Marjorie sOddenly. said it must be ten .c'clock, and. she must go in. " I shall speak to Mrs. Norton -to-morrow," Guise said, as •he lcd the girl back towards, the house. But, emerging from the shrubbery into the broad light of a moon sailing in a cloudless sky, they came face. tâ. face with Mrs. Norton. The lady stopped dead. "Miss Vernerl " she said. Guise stepped fcr- ward. "Pardon me,". he said, - courteously, "if I speak for Miss 'Verner, who has honoured me by promising to become ray wife." - • --
-" Indeed ! said Mrs. Ncrton, sarcastically. "But I hardly think it becoming in Miss Verner to.. moot von clanclf!stinelv. and at nit"

This was the first time, Mrs. Norton, at my earnest and urgent request. It is Lot her fault or mine that I .cannot meet her in the ordinary way.',' 'lt is no concern of mine," said the lady, coldly; "I admit that I have no fault in general

to find with Miss Verner; and if you and she choose to marry on .a pittance—" "A pittance of some £40,000 a year," inter- rupted Guise, coolly.', • A startled exclamation broke from Marjorie. Mrs. Norton cried, sharply: "What do you mean? A jest!." "No," he said; "a test. Eut, to maim full confession, I lost my heart to. Miss Verner he. (ore _I came here; but as I was in some measure pledged to Ella, I thought I would put her to the proof. You knew the result.",
"And you consider such conduct horr- ourabl,e? " said Mrs. Nortcn, almost choking vith mortification.
it i 9. If a .r..cman loves my money ar.d,not me. the shall be no wife Of mine. come, .‘,rarjorie. I shell not trespass upon your hOsi,i- tality beyond to-night, Mrs. Norton."
Poor Ella! She could never hope to win such a prize as had been within her grasp had she (lily known itthe prize winch .I,tlarjorle, not gained.•

"What would have become of me," Maurice Guise said to his young wife on their wedding. say, "if we had. not met as we did, and you witched my hea i. from me in the long hours we passed together in the little waiting-room. You never suspected that—how should you, any more than you suspected that the poor man who wooed you was rich; but richer in pining you, sweetheart,,- than if all the wealth of Golconda were his I"- _ _ _

div.head: CRUSADE AGAINST BETTING.
div.p: CRUSADE AGAINST BETTING.
Smart Penalty at Warrington.

The Warrington police are continuing their crnsade against street betting, and at the Borough Police Court, on Saturday, before Mr. J. W. Hayward (presiding), Aldermen Tienion and Bennett, Messrs. R. T. Fair- cleugh, A. J. Jolley and Dr. Markel, William Green, , aged 18, of 18, Knutsford-road, was charged with frequenting -Litherland's-yard, off Knutsford-road, for Ithe purpose of belting on June 30th, and July let and 2nd. Mr. Steel appeared for the defendant and pleaded ' gnilty. I The Chief Constable said that on Tuesday lest ' Detectives Metcalfe and Clough were detailed to keep observation in Litherland's-yard, off Knutsford-rtrad. They took up a position at 11.50 in the morning and remained there until 2.45 in the afternoon. They saw defendant. in the yard, but he creme in and out quite frequently. During that period 81 persons were seen to band to him slips of paper and cash, namely, 47 men, 15 women, 14 boys and five, girls. Some of the boys and girls were very young and some were without boots and stockings. 1-le did not suggest that they were taking slips for themselves. The probability was that in most cases .they were taking Ahem for their par eats or for other grown-up people. On Wednesday, July Ist; the eame.officers kept observation in the same place from 12.20 until -2.50, and during that time defendant had interviews with no fewer than 92 persons, and from each of them he took one or more slips of paper and money. The officers had a very strong pair of field glasses, and they could even diecern the coins. Therewere 59 men, ten women, 13 boys cud ten girls. In this case come of the boys and girls were quite young. On Thursday, July 2nd, defendant was charged with frequenting the same place. The officers saw him come at 12.35 and at 1.15 by arrangement. Detective Woollacott proceeded in disguise down the yard, and arrested the defendant. -On that occasion 13 men, one woman, one boy, and two girls handed him slips of Ipaper and meney. There bad been quite a number of complaints with regard to betting in this particular neighbourhood. He hoped the Bench would deal with the cases in such a manner as would not as a deterrent to other people. Mr. Steel said the desire of the police and of the Bench was to put down street Letting asi far as poesible and he quite agreed that it was nn abominable nuisance. The prisoner etes the son of Mr. Thomas Green, a notorious Letting man, and tie (Mr. Steel) was using his position as an advocate on behalf of the young man with a view to putting dowu the vice of betting.'" Ho had had a long convereation with the lather, 'who had promised that if the Bench would deal with his. son in the way he (Mr. Steel) was about to suggest, that from that time forth he would not boa party to betting at all. He (Mr. Steel) suggested that the Bench should impose a nominal penalty in the first case, and that with regard to the other cases the Bench should deal with the prisoner under the Probation of Offenders Act, by which he could enter into recognizances for any length of time not exceeding three years. The Bench then retired from the Court to consider their deciaion, and on their return, The Chairman said : The unanimous decision of the Retch is that the defendent be fined £lO and costs in each circa, or cne month's irnprisonnaent in each care in default. The fines and costs amounted to £3l Is. The Chief Con-stable asked what was to be done with the Letting slips found on the defendant. Mr. Steel asked that they should be handed over to tke defendant, who had every desire to be honourable. After some further discussion it was decided that the slips should be confiscated.

div.head: HINTS FOR THE HOME.
div.p: HINTS FOR THE HOME.

To E.Emovsr POTS EnOn VP A S RING FABRICS.— Before sending to the laundry, rub the yolk of an egg on the spots and this will remove them. A SLICE of common onion rubbed on the place is a certain cure for a wasp sling., If the sting be in the threat or mouth an onion ,sivettild be slowly chewed aud swallowed. Tstutt SALt—When salt is dried for table use it shvuld be allowed to grs4w cold before being put in the salt-cellars, as if this is nut done the salt will cake to;et her in lumps. Buass rings sewn on to muslin curtains are better than the patent 'safety-pms stuck into them, as the rings do away with the fear °trusty marks appearing at the top .of the curtain. , FbAncur, garments should not be allowed to become very dirty, as if they have to have hard rubbing it cileh ruins them. They 'really ought not be rubbed to all, but only washed in soapsuds by dipping theta qui,kly up and down until they look clean. scrubb!ng floors and tables donut use soda, for it makes the boards a bad colour and does not eetin better than soap and plenty of cold water. The boards should be scrubbed the way of the grain, and not -round and round. If cleaned in this manner they will soon be a good colour. Should they be greased at all, then a little soda and hot 'water will be needed first of all to remove it.

110 W TO CLEAN G....);=, AT HOME.—Dny from any chemist three pennyworth of benzoline; take a clean piere of flannel and rub over the soiled Rift of the gloves with benzoline. If the gloves are first put on the hands it will render it easy to clean them in'every part. All dirt will be removed and the gloves look almost like new. Take great care to keep the benzo- line away from a fire or gas, as it easily ignites and evaporates._ .

ROLLED Ox TONGUE.—ChonPe a very prime tongue which has been pickled according to taste, and, after trimming it neatly, put it, into a saucepan of lukewarm water, add some carrots, onions, celery, &c., all riloghly chopped, a bench of savoury herbs, a tea- spoonful of peppercorns, and at dozen cloves; bring very slowly to the toil, after which skin carefully and simmer very gently until the meat is thoroughly cooked. When done enough, remove the skim, trial the root neatly; takeout the bones, and roll the tongue, - fat inwards, as tightly as possible, then press it into a round mould, just barely large enongh to hold it, pet a heavy • weight on top, and leave it untouched until thoroughly cold; then tnru it out, 'brush it over with two or three coats of glaze, taking care to let one dry before adding. another, and serve on a dish- paper tastefully garnished with suitable items.— "Marie," in the Agricakura/ geti-eite. COLLA RED OR MARBLED Banc.—Take the requisite qeentity of the thln flank of beef, which has lain in a guod tellable pickle front five to eight days, aecord- ing to taste, and, after carefully removing the bones, by the meat out flat, sin downwards, on a board, and beat it gently until as nearly equal in thickness as possible, then cover the surface with alternate layers of hard-boiled eggs cut in slices, rashers of prime, streaky bacon, finely chopped parsley, and a few chopped nmshrooms or piekled walnuts, each layer being Seasoned appropriately, and roll the meat no very tightly and neatly, sect:ring it in shape by a literal binding of white tape, after which sew it up finely in a strong cloth, and put it into a saucepan of boiling water. Boil for not longer than a minnte,then draw the Pan on one side, and simmer very gently indeed, until, when pierced by a fine skewer or a knitting needle, the meat feels sufficiently, tender, when it should be taken up, well drained, and placed between two dishes with a heavy weight on top; leave it so over-night in a cool piece, then next, day remove the Wrapping and binding, and coat the meat nicely with good glaze. Before tLe latter is ()bite set, sprinkle it lightly with .a mixture of finely-chopped parsley and sifted egg yolk, then when required cut a tiny slice from each end of the bee', so as to show the dainty appearance of the interior, and serve garnished round about with a full close border of parsley, upon which is arranged fancifully cut slices of fresh lemon and bright, red boiled -beetroot. MOULDED lisars,—lf the remains of cooked meats,, Teal and ham,, for instance, are being used for moulding, a most attractive dish, both as regards aprearance and taste, can be. made as follows: First of all prepare • 'some economi- cal aspic jelly, which is simply highly- flavoured stock carefully cleared in the usual way and mixed with a sullteient quantity of French sheet gelatine to render it quite firm when cold ; then when cool, but still liquid, pour a little of this into a'plain mould of the requisite size and thoroughly coat the inside, after which sprinkle lightly with finely chopped parsley, and leave the mould in a cool place until the decoration is nicely set. • When ready fill in with the veal, cut in very small, neat pieces, the bum, cut in tiny thin slices, hard-boiled eggs cut in slices or small pieces, and a sprinkling of chopped parsley. Arrange the various - ingt%dients quite loosely and in tasteful order, Bo that when turned out the different colours may contrast prettily, then pour in as much aspic—which has been kept in a liquid state—as the mould will hold, and set the latter into a cool place to stiffen. Serve turned out on a cbsh-paper, garnished with a rind of fresh green parsley, and accompanied by a well-mixed, daintily- dressed salad., Other kinds of meat can, of course, be substituted for the veal if more convenient.

SOMMER CllTlAM.—Dissolve a quarter of an Mince of gelatine in half a pint of milk, and sweeten to taste. IVlten it little cooled, add a gill of thick cream, attcl stir it till mixal. Place some stewed fruit of any kind preferred at the bottom of a dish, and, when the cream is almost set, pour it gently over the fruit. Set the dish on one side for three hours, then stick it with blanched pistachio nuts. As this cream is perfectly smooth and flat, it can be -ornamented in many ways for a variety.—Loa don Journal. To keep butter cool and sweet in hot weather, fill a box with sand to within an inch or two of the top; sink the butter-jar in the sand, and then thoroughly saturate the sand with cold water. Cover the box down tightly from the air. It may be kept in the pantry. . _ _ _

SPIOLINA PUDDING.—BoiI half a pint of milk with three limipx,of sugar. When boiling, sift in a dessert- spoonful of semolina; boil for five minutes. Take it off the fire. and when cool stir in the yolk of an egg and the white beaten to a stiff froth. Bake in a good oven for twenty minutes. Ir your face feels sore and uncomfortable after being out in the wind, rub a little cold-cream well in directly you come indoors. Leave it on fOrten min- utes, then wipe off and bathe your face—first with warm water, and then with cold.- Dry thoroughly, and give a final rub with a soft chamoise-leather. To vary the monotony of meat broth and beef tea, take half a pint of chicken broth, and thicken it slightly with ground sago, season it to taste with pepper, salt, and a little grated nutmeg, and add a tablespoonful and a half of thick cream. A. very nourishing soup is the result, and one which is not commonly known. To CGEAN A WITITE STRAW ITAT.--Stir a teaspoon- ful of powdered sulphur into the juice of a lemon. Brush the mixture on to (he hit with a toothbrush, and when gnite clean place it under a tap and let cold wafer run over it to free it from the sulphur. Dry in the air, Lut not in the-sunshine. Let the hat rest on a table or-other flat surface while drying, so as to keep the brim Oat.

div.head: CORONER BUSY.
div.p: THE CORONER BUSY.
Far Ixpasts at Warringtoa.
Mr. S. Brighouse, County Coroner, held fonr invssts at the Warrington Pollee Station on Monday evening. SEQUEL:TO A WORICS ACCIDENT.

The adjourned int-1,14y into the circumstances attend- ing the death of William Fletcher (69), JB7, Berney- road; who died in the Haien Hospital on June 2Sth, was first held. Mr. F. G.Taylor (Nlessrs.Renry Greenatl and Co.) represented Messrs. Pearson and Knowles, and Ur. • Sumner, KAI. Lispeotor of Factories, WAS also present. Abraham Hankinson, 82, Scott-street, crane driver in the moulders' dere Irtment at Messrs. Pearson and Knowles' works, sairl decoased was employed as a moulders labourer. Sotno time about Christmas deceased was assisting in casting and some molten metal spilled and dropped into his clog. Witness asked deceased to take the clog off and have his foot attended to, but deceased refused, saying " it was nothing." He continued to follow his employment for some days, aitd then startgd losing odd days, complain- ing that the foot nag worse than he thonght it was. In February he was obliged to leave work altogether. In answer to nr. Taylor witness said that miny years ago deceased told him be was surto:lin from diabetes. Dr. Corker, resident assistant medical °fazes at the Workhouse hospital, said that when admitted to the institution deceased was suffering from diabetes end gangrene of the foot. Witness was told that the state of the foot was caused by some burning sand dropping into his boot whilst at work. The primary cause of death was diabetes and the secondary cense diabetic gangrene. He was of opinion that the injury would not have caused any ill effects if deceased had not been suffering from diabetes at the into but ho also con- sidered that deceased would have lived longer had it not been for the injury. I Dr. Hodgkinson said the diabetic garigreno probably hastened the man's death. Witness was not prepared to say that the gangrene was caused by a burn. The in in might have been cutting a corn and made-the toe bleed, and that would be suflicient to set up gangrene. The Coroner said he did not think there was ever a story in tbis world that had so many connecting links as this., Although deceased was suffering from diabetes and would no doubt have died from it in due time, his death was accelerated by the gangrene of the foot. The jury returned a verdict of Accidental death." TANNERY FATALITY.

, The next inquiry wis concerning the death of John Henry McMahon (33), 15, Hardy-street, tanner's labourer, who fell into a pit of liquor at the tannery of Messrs. Randall Bros., Ltd., Tanner's-lane, on the pre- vihs Thursday.—Mr. Browne appeared for the firm, Mr. Steel for the relatives, and Mr. Sumner, Factory Inspector, also watched the proceedings.—Mr. Browne said the firm %ere exceedingly sorry that the accident had occurred, and uished to give every information in their power. Patrick Ryan, tanners' labourer, 70, Lythgass-lans, stated that at 7.45 on Thursday morning he and the deceased wore engaged in removing some wet skins from one tan pit to another. To do that they had to cross a pit over which was a cover on a pl.ink. Deceased was standir'pi on the.cover and witness was wheeling a barrow full of skins. Deceased was assisting him by guiding the barrow in the front. IVben they got to the board over the pit, the wheel of the barrow struck the cover and it gave ray. Deceased fell back wards into the pit and the skins, weighing 2 cwt., fell on the top of him. Witness haw," on to the barrow. The pit was about 3 feet deep. Dr." Adams was rent for and afterwards deceased was able to walk home.

Mr. Browne said the accident was absolatoly inexpli- cable, as such a thing had never occurred before. Reginald Hamilton Smith, foreman tanner,s2,Walton- road, Stockton Heath, said that in his fifteen years' experience he bad never known a sichilai accident to happen and he could not accou.at for it. Ile pit con- tained tannic acid. _ _

f Dr. Adams said he arrived at the works alma two minutes after receivinginforrnation. If it had been a case of drowning only deceased was quite resuscitated. Wittiest, gave instructions for him to be taken home and again saw him at 10 o'clock when he was worse. On 'calling again about 11.30 or 11.45 he saw that the-end was very near, and deceased died about ten minutes after be left the house. Witness was of opinion that death was doe to the absorption of the tannir,- -nterial which bhd been drawn into the lungs and ret.ulted in paralysis of the heart's action. A verdict of "Accidental death" was returned. A FATAL DAVIE.

An inquest was then held on Hobert flleMillan (IGL painter, 4, Brook Place, Latchford, who was drowned in : the river the previous Thursday afternoon. 11,-.seesed's wife said he left home at 1.15 to go for a wa: . I John Charles Crutchley, tram conductor, 25, Fir. ,; tee- : street' said he met deceased at the Black Bear IL., :.)y appointment at 2.43. They had a drink together and I then set out NV jai the intention of hiring a boat at I Howley and going for a row to Paddington. However, they saw some men bathing in /the river and they decided to do the same. Witness first to enter the water and swam three parts of th. across the river and bark again. Deceased then .dived into the water and struck out, "giving witness the impression ' that he could swim quite well. When he had got half way witness asked him to turn back but be said he was going aerogs. Soon afterwards he appeared to be in trouble and when witness asked him what was the ' matter he said " I'm done." Witness got hold of , ; ceceased's left hand and struck out for the shore but , when he had made a couple of strokes deceased went down and Frnsped witness by the ankle. Witness , had to kick out and make him loose his : hold. He then got deceased by the wrist and they. managed to get half the distance to the shore. Witness was done up,so he started floating, still holding deceased by the wrist. Eventually deceased clutched him by the • shoulder and they went down. Thera was a strong , under-current, and witness called for help to EOlllO young men who were on the bank. One of them entered the water but he had to go back, as ha was done up. I Another man then threw a lifebuoy but it fell short. He then throw a rope which witness was just able to I grasp, and he was dragged ashore. I The Coroner: Were you both sober? . Witness) Yes.

Joseph Shaw, lock keeper at Manor Lack, said the water was about 15 feet deep where the men were bathing. Witness got Crutchley out, by moans of the rope, but deceased sank. Crutchley wanted to go back to the deceased, but witness would not let him as he was completely done up, and would certainly have been drowned if he bad again attempted to save the deceased. The Coroner : Ile had a near shave.

A verdict of "'Accidentally drowned " was returned. The Coroner said it was <Fate clear Crutchley did all he could and ran very near risking his own life. If ha had been a selfish man he could have left the deceased altogether.

div.head: FATAL FALL DOWNSTAIRS.
div.p: FATAL FALL DOWNSTAIRS.

I The last inquiry concerned the death of Meshach Tomlinson (47), 231, Winwick-road, a mill furnaceman employed by Messrs. Pearson and Knowles, who sustained fatal injuries by falling downstairs at his • home. IDeceased's widow stated that on Thursday night she . end deceased bad been marketing and their returned , borne at 10.10. They had been in the house a few minutes when their three-year-Ad daughter, who was in bed, began to cry, and deceased went upstairs to bring her down. As he was returning he had got about half-way when his foot slipped end he and the child j fell to the bottom of the stairs. Deceased was bleed- ing profusely from the left ear and Dr. Ferguson was , rummoned and found he was suffering from a fractured skull. He died at 1.25 on Friday morning. The child I was slightly injured. A verdict of " Accidental death" was returned.

Th 3 PiTo333d NOW OrfiebS

A Meeting of this Board was hell at the W.rringtrn Workhouse on 'iVedaesclay, the Ray. T. R. Matthews presidins. There were alss present :—Mrs. Simpson, Nlrs. Collingwood, Miss Broadbent.. Rao'. M. Ryon, Dr. Murray, Messrs. N. L. Bent, .J. Billinge, NV. Gill, W. Farness, W. C. Brooks, A. Brooks, M. W. Scion, It. Forshaw, R. Bolton, W. Flannagan, A Bottoraley (clerk), R. W. Peaconlc (assistant clerk), J. F. A vbory (master). and A. Wright (superintendent of the Cottage Homes),

A: CURIOUS REWEST. The MASTER reported that an inspector of the Board of Agriculture visited the Workhouse and wanted three pigs to be killed in order to satisfy his deptrtment that the:e was no swine fever. fie (Nit. Awbery) refused to pArtnit this to be done without the consent of the Gutrdians, as the pigs wore all in good health and appeared to be thriving welL (Laughter.) The matter was referred to the flOuse Committee. GUARDIA.NS AS CRICKETERS.

At a meeting -Ofthe ilons Gn-m-i1tee....1; was decided that a cricket match lie arranged between the Guardians and oMeials of the Warrington Thursday team. This was agreed to. RE-ARRANGEMENT OF TIIE OFFICES. . . -

The Special Committee appointed to consider the question of office accommodation recommended that all the rooms on the first floor be used by the'ofticers of the Guardians oaly ; the store room for stationery to be converted into a private office of the clerk, the room: occupied by the collector to be used as a store room, the room lately occupied by the assistant clerk to be used by the collector and other °Ulcers of the Union when work is required to be done by them at the Union offices, and the room I ttely occupied by Mr. Sutton to be the clerk's keneril elm It was also recommended that Mr. Sutton and Mr. Kerfoot be transferred to the buildings tenanted by the Rural District Council, subject to the approval of the District Council, and that Mr. Peacock, assistant clerk, be requested to resign his appointment as deputy superin- tendent registrar, the terms of his appointment being that he must devote the whole of his time to the duties of the Guardians.

Mr. BELLINGE, in moving the adoption of the report, said it was the wish of the committee to make their offices in Bawsey-street distinct for Poor Law parposes only. Mr. Sutton had intimated that he had no objection to occupying an o:Hce in the Rural District Council's rooms.

Mr. FortgESS second%d and the report was agreed to. THE PRoPOSED NEW OFFICES. QUEEN-STREET SITE NOT APPROVED. Mr. Btr,rANos ollerd :—" That the'lleard adopt the Queen-street plot of land for the erection of new offices iSrc., thereon, if still available, subject to the subsequent approval thereof by the Local Government Board." Ile said he had beOn advissd that it would be better to defer the :natter, bet he was not of that opinion. He thought they were all agreed that now offices wcre required, but there might be some slight difference of opinion as ti where they should be built. After con- sidering the many sites brought before the nutice of the committee, he could not think of a better one to meet their requirements than the laud in Queen-street. It would en ible them to have in the on building, offices for the Guardians, the relieving °lacers, registration offices, and Rural District Council offices, and the com- mittee were informed by the architects that the site lent itself to the purpose, particularly for relief offices. If the Guardians could become owners of the land at an equitable price he thought they ought to acquire it. The a IternAive schf-me in the minds of some of the Guardians was to build offices at the Work- house. They could build offices far relief purposes ft there, but the Registrar woul I not appr eof registra- tion offices being_at the Workhouse, so ey wont.' have to be erected elsewhere. Under the pr sant conditions the adrnistisf r ition of relief could not have that atten- tion and scrutiny which it required. The price of .the land as recorded by the Clerk at the last meeting was about £1,300 and a two-storey building would meet all requirements. There was no enonler to the motion which therefore fell to the ground.

OLD-AGE PENSIONS. The CLE3K reported the receipt of resolations frrrn the Guardians of the Pari‘th of Birmingham 041 the Oid Age Pensions Bill. Be said the matter was engaging the attention of the Poor 7.4.t•i, Unions Association and he did not think groat good was done by individual boards sending up such resolutions. They could recom- mend that the letter bo refe.red to the Poor Law Unions Association for consider ttion. Mr. A. Lino :Its said thlt mig'it ho an opportunity to notify the new- clerk that till Board harl hitherto rigorously abstained from anything which was of a po:itical character. Of course they were experts on that kind of thing hut he thought the knowledge they had was hest used outside the Board and not inside. The matter then dropped. TREAT FOR THE CHILDREN. A letter was read from Mrs. Frost, Grappenhall Bell, inviting the Workhouse children to tea at G rappenhal -
T 1 Board Board readily granted permission for the children to go.

A PRIVATE BANKING ACCOUNT. INQUIRY WANTED. , Mr. W. C. BROOXS said that some six weeks ago the Board resolved itself into committee to discuss the question of the private banking account which had hitherto been in existence. On his own propositior, seconded by Mr. VORNES3, it was decided to have a full inquiry into that account extending over five years, in order to ascertain all the receipts and payments, lie wanted to know why effect had not been given to the resolution. - -
The CLcaT I have no knowledge of stth a reselu• tion. If there is one on the hooks T will look into it,.

Mr. Bnoogs : It was carried with -only t;;; 'dis- sentients. On inquiries I find there have been no steps taken at the hank to fulfil the proposition. The CLERK (after referring to the hooks) : lam afraid there is not such a resolution on the minutes. I should have done this myself had I known of it, but it is news to me.

The CH.unmA.N : Mv impression was that our coaling to the conclusion to h-and over and put an end to the private account put an end to the whole thing. Mr. BROOKS moved that there be a full inveEtlgatirin of the account extending over five years, showing the income and exponditure. Mr. FORST-TAW seconded. __ •

Mr. Br thought such an inquiry woold serve no metal purpose now but would very likely fill the public mouth with a scandal. Mrs. CULLING WOOD said that, as a new Corner, it seemed to be a strange thing. that when a gentleman had worked for them all those years, just as he was leaving them, they appeared to throw a slur on his methods. Why not have done it ten or five years ago ? Mr. FonsttAw said the resolution was in no sense reflecting on the late clerk. They had not the slightest doubt that they would be furnished with the informa- tion and it was on the late clerk's behalf that he seconded the motion, because to bury it now would be dishonourable to Mr. Sutton and to the Board. He (Mr. Forshaw),did not know until lately that there was a private amount and he thought many more were in the same position. Mr. BiivT : I hope you won't get the information. Mr. NV. C. BitooKs : The bite clerk expressed a desire that it should be furnished and said he would welcome it.

Mr. BENT The matter shoalsl nat be reaped up. It should die a natural deith. If there is any balance at the bank it should be put to our credit. Miss BROA.DEEXT : It MU the late Clerk who told us about it.
Oa vote boing taken the proposition was carriei by 10 rotes to 3.

div.head: IN MIDST OF BUSY LIFE SENDS LETTER OF PRAISE
div.p: IN MIDST OF BUSY LIFE SENDS LETTER OF PRAISE

DUNKIRK VICARAGE, FAVERSHAM, July 10, 1907 'Dear Sir: I am very busily en- gaged in preparation for the reopening of our parish_church which has delayed my reply to your recent letter. I TAT tell you that I have been vicar of this parish since January 1854, and am now in ray eighty-fifth year. My ailment affected my face and forehead. It commenced five or six years ago and I had recourse to several remedies and consulted two physicians. After a, while I happened to read an adver- tisement about Cuticura and deter- mined to give it a trial. So I began . with the Cuticura Soap, then purchased Cuticura Ointment, then added the .
