div.head: EXAMINER.
div.p: THE EXAMINER.
JULY 11th. 1908.

Those of us who were A WILD opposed to the BJer War PROPOSAL, had many sound grounds for opposition. One of @ur contentions was that the policy which led up the South African conflict would also lead to a demand for Protection and to another demand for Conscription. It has been admirably said that Prophecy is the most gratuitous form of human error. But this prophecy happens to have come true. Tiae Tariff Reform policy was the immediate outcome of South Africa, and tho demand for Conscription, now disguised under

the name of national military training, is its corollary. If there was one lesson more than another to be learned from the Baer War it was that we were in im:nediate uoed of an entire reorganisation of the army. Obviously the great

. need of the nation was a fighting force officered by . 4len who had made themselves acquainted with , their duties under all conditions, and backed up .• by a War Office which had prepared itself against all eventualities. What we did not need was a ;. Prime Minister who could not sleep at nights z because the country had been hastily denuded of ' ammunition, a War Secretary who did not read despatches, and military advisers who thought - that the Boers could be "polished off" in three : Months. Just, however, as it was considered necessary to , stalt the Tariff Reform movement in order to . • divert public attention from the disastrous state of things .g produced in South Africa, so it was thought to be ingenious to side-track the national demand , for Army reform in a Conscriptionist direction. It la particularly noteworthy that Lord ROBERTS, ' who failed to reform the War Office, and ' left the Army much as it was before, should . be the first of the conscriptionists. It is ' equally characteristic of the origin of the Movement that he should have an energetic supporter in the gloomy-minded Lord MILNER. , There are some members of Parliament—they 11 * are fortunately very few—who are evidently con- ' vineed that the Conscriptionist movement has made great progress. Tneir House of Commons Champion is Captain KINCAID-SMITH, a pretty ,geuerally malcontent Liberal, who this week cr°llght in a Bill to make national training in the Territorial Army compulsory. That principle is, of Course, only a small step towards the ultimate seeuvde ;r a lb unat i lilt. 0 wso uiltd wroaui sl de a imposete rri tao rvi aa Is t forceburd eonf on the taxpayers, and it would gravely hamper - industry and commerce by withdrawing the man- hood of the nation for military training at the time of life when we are all acquiring our best , experience in our various callings. Captain Soma proposes to draw the whole of us , into his net, with the exception, as it would seem, .i3l nembers of Parliament and habitual drunkards. Ile examples set np for us, a great military Ration, with an enormous Empire to defend, are , the peoples who play at soldiering. We are to * look to Norway and to Switzerland for inspiration , Itnd teaching. What does Switzerland, what does 14.0rway, may we be permitted to ask, want with , an army at all ? What could either country do J against an enemy that was formidable and - in , earnest ? The best security of such ( )tates is to be found in international gilarantees or understandings. They may Play at soldiering, even in a quite impressive Manner, but to adduce them as examples to our . ,13eives is not merely ridiculous, but grotesque. "hat the country is not being converted to Con- lerintion, as some people affect to believe, is clear. enough from the reception by the House of 2mtirnons of Captain KINCAID-SMITH'S Bill. 'there were only two speeches, one for and one tsgainst the measure being introduced under the en minutes rule. But the one speech against 1 ;vas quite enough. The Bill was not exactly taw. ,hed out of the House ; but it was hustled out, the numbers in favour of its introduction being 34, against 250. It is painful to think, however, that : there should be thirty-four members in favour of °O ill-digested a proposal. •

The Town Council on TEE Foot-BRIDGE Tuesday sanctioned the AT HowLEv. construction of a suspension • bridge over the river at "'ley at an estimated cost of £6OO. Only the il3llghest of sketch designs is available for inspec- #Lon, and Alderman Bannett waxed sarcastic about :lie temporary nature of the structure, his conten- . being that a proper vehicular bridge would be ) soundest and most economical scheme in the run. Still, it was unkind of him to suggest rat the Committee "appeared to be getting an tr,°ntoonger's catalogue and buying a bridge as m 3 o'3' would a watering-can.' time is not 45Portune for a permanent vehicular bridge at , a "v, ley, and if the now foot-bridge tempts R„low more thousands into Victoria Park, at the same time provides a shorter i4)4te for foot-passengers and cyclists between watehford and Howley it will soon have proved its ,I,,Qrtb. Before any more elaborate scheme can be • ta'veloped in this quarter, Warrington Bridge %list be dealt with. That is the most urgent and faletltial improvement with which the town is aci, as a public duty. It has been blocked and most Ponod for years, and one could wish for the ft7etit of a stray Nihilist with the inevitable bomb °rder to disperse the difficulties which have so stood in the way of either a new or a widened

It is rather a curious Acoin- cidence that while we were "AultirrcroN, commenting last week on I tin , , the need for pushing War- 4"sa claims as a manufacturing centre, there a resolution on the Town Council minutes in I

the name of Councillor Perriborton which proposed the formation of a" Towns Committee" with this identical object. The resolution was passed unanimously at the meeting on Tuesday, and.a isum of £5O granted to the Committee for immedi- ate expenses. We hope an eftort will be made to get into touch with some of the foreign maul tc- , turers who will deem it necessary to establish works in this country under the new Patents Act. Warrington is the spot ideal, with its wJaderful railway and water-carriage facilities, and abundance of suitable laud. We should welcome almost any kind of works whic`i would find employment and contribute substanti- ally to rateable values. A. slightly discordant note was struck by Alderman Bennett, who deprecated the idea of making Warrington into a huge Widnes or a bigger St. Helens. He wood rather have "less prosperity and a pleasanter town to live in." We hardly think the Alderman displayed his customary foresight whets he ventured on this somewhat premature warning. Whatever manufactures become associated with the town there is no reason why we should sink to the level of drab ugliness which is a characteristic of Widnes. Even Widnes conld be made into a nice town with its present class of mannfactures if it could only he planned afresh ! With the rapid development of town-planning facilities there is no need for manufacturs to drag sordid ugliness in its train. Why, even the smoke can be eliminated, as tne Aldtrman should surely know. Then again, we shall never get a pleasanter town by the aid of less prosperity—a fact which should he equally patent on the slightest reflection. Warrington has missed its way in the past, and if advertising will make up seine of the leeway let us advertise, advertise!

The R9yalist cause in France Flaxen AND cannot be said to have been ROYALISM. particularly fortunate in recent years, either in its actions or its exponents. The Republican form of Government has achieved a certain amount ef tangible success since the events which brought it into existence. It came into being as the choice of the delegates of the people, but yet not by any very emphatic selection, since the Assembly at Bordeaux might very easily have chosen to restore the Monarchy. The history of the last thirty-seven years—though it con- tains much that demonstrates that weakness exists in this as in other systems—has ehewn that France did not choose unwisely. Tile Due d'Orlans, however' seems to think that the present moment is one favourable to the pressure of the claim of the Bourbons to be reinstated on the throne. He has, in the columns of the " Matin " published what he calls " Toe Pro• gramme of the King "—a manifesto setting forth what the Nlonarchy would be prepared to do for France. The idea appears to be that, owing to the dispute between the Government and the Church in the Republic, the cause of the Royalists has made sufficiently solid progress in recent years to justify the hope that a change may be induced in the attitude of the people. Toe Due promises that the Monarchy, if it were restored, would maintain the universal Kith. ige ; and, so far from menacing the present liberties of the people, would procure them others which th e Republic has not dared to concede. Ii addition to that, he promises a better system of representa- tive Government than the present. Oa tie whole, we do not fancy a manifesto of this sort will have much effect. France has had sad experience of the danger and disadvantage of changes of this Iritid, and in the present condition of aff.tirs there is no question that she would weaken herself by a revolution, even of a peaceful character. PALACE AND HIPPODROME.

Another high-class programme has been provided for the patrons of the Palace and Hippodrome this week. Not only has the standard of excellence bcen well-maintained lately, but it really appears to be going up. Some of the best variety shows possible have been given in Warrington_ of late. This week the bill is beaded by May Moore-Duprez, who is one of the best Dutch girl impersonators we have seen. Her patter is smart and her humour infectious to a degree, while such songs as " Gretchen " and " Louisa Schmidt "always bring down the house. In addition to being a " Jolly Dutch •Girl," May Moore- Duprez is also a jolly good da.ncer, and the clatter of her wooden sabots makes merry music. Quite the best pair of acrobats we have seen for a long time are the Kremka Brothers. Their's is a turn punctuated by cheers, as one remarkable feat after another is performed with a celerity and neatness which indicate muscle, mind, and training. All their work is done ' without apparatus, which makes it specially meritori- ous. There is plenty of dancing in the programme, I and both the San Remo girls, and the five Bombays I display wonderful agility and expertness. The ' former make a speciality of tumbling and danciug combined, while the latter excel in the art of com- bined step-dancing. Their singing is not a strong point, and it is a matter for surprise t o us why so many accomplished dancing and speciality troupes deem it necessary to introduce singing, for which they have no special qualification. It must be the fashion of the time! The four Maisamos introduce far and away the best turn as eccentric musicians that we have yet seen on the boards. So many of these performers are merely eccentric and not musical, but the Maisamos are refreshingly clever and original in all respects. A comedy and burlesque interlude is given by the Kirbys, who provoke roars of laughter. Miss Edie Reynolds, a London violinist, plays a couple of selections with skill and taste, and George Lawrence, light comedian, sings songs which appeal to those who love something with a chorus. Mr. Widdop's orchestra plays some admirable selections, among them a pleasing overture from the pen of Mr. G. D. Bradbury, the popular manager. Mr. H. A. Freeman is deservedly applauded for a piccolo solo, " The Comet," which brightens the " interval." Raymond's bio-tableaux, as usual, end the bill with capital pictures. On Thursday afternoon a special matinee, in aid of the staff outing, was held. An excellent array of talent had been got together, the members of the company appearing this week being supported by other well-known artistes, including several local ladies and gentlemen. There was a crowded house, and the performance went with a merry swing throughout. Mr. G. D. Bradbury, the manager, expressed the thanks of the staff to the artistes and to the public for their generous supp )rt. NEXT WEEK'S PROGRAMIIE.

Another highly interesting programme is announced for next week. The bill is headed by Richard Corbin and his wonderful performing dogs, whose entertainment will be well worth seeing. J. F. Elliston will present the great laughing hit, " The Art of Deception " with that inimitable comedian, Shaun Glenville, as " The Tramp." The other artistes will be :—Victor Travers, eccentric comedian I Mayme Cannon, comedienne ; The Florias, wonderful novelty equilibrists and comedy slack wire artistes ; The Avolos, originators of what is described as the greatest acrobatic and gymnastic novelty of the age ; Les Belles Anaericaine, vocalists and expert dincors ; Edie Gasson in " The Escap vie," tby prlniss ion by Mr. Monkhouse), assisted by Alexander Wills.

div.head: Cat in the Oven.
div.p: A Cat in the Oven.

Al the Warrin-gton Borough. Court, yesterday, James Kelly, Cropper's-brow was summoned for cruelly ill-treating a cat on June 25th. He pleaded not guilty.—The evidence was to the effect that on the night in question two men named Michael Scully and Frederick Dawson were sitting on Cropper's-brow, and they saw the defendant enter a lodging-house. Immediately afterwards they heard the screams of a eat, and on going into the kitchen they found that the cat's hind legs had been badly burned i through having been n the hot oven. Defendant was the only one in the house. Scully drowned the cat. Defendant denied that he had anything to do with the cat being in the oven. When he entered the house he heard the cat screaming, and found it in the oven, and he immediately let it out.—The Mayor (Alderman Smethurst) remarked that there was not sufficient evidence to connect the defendant with having put the cat in the oven, but whoever did so ought to have , twelve months and a flogging. The case was dis- missed.

the reform of the treatment of the poor generally. Strong criticisms have been passed by Mr. Balfour on the want of detail in the Bill. lie is sorely grieved that the way of working the Old Age Pensions has not been set forth elaborately in the measure. This would have given the Opposition a glorious chance of !exercising their ingenuity in criticism, and the result would have been not only perilous to this measure, but to much other legislation of this session. But apart from that, the scheme of the Government to leave the Bill as loose as it could safely be left, and to settle all detail by regulations which can be altered Ifrom time to time as experience may show to be [necessary without any anaandin:,° measure by Parlia- ment, is by far the wiser. It is also the course recommended by experience ia the Colonies. The Old Age Pensions Bill is a big achievement, and will make the names of Hr. Asquith and Hr. Lloyd-George shine in the annals of social legislation.

div.head: POLITICS OF THE WEEK.
div.p: THE POLITICS OF THE WEEK.

[BY OUR LONDON CORRESPONDENT.] As this week ends, Ministers are preparing for the winding-up of the first part of the session of 1908. IFor the next three (it may be four) weeks, all rules as I to hours will be suspended, so that no advantage can be taken of the clock to hinder the programme of the Government. All the time of the House will be at the Government's command ; the work still to be done will be mapped out with that businesslike precision which has distinguished the administration of Hr. !Asquith, and Parliament will separate for a brief i holiday, having advanced by 1 ing steps the solution of some of the moat important social problems of our ' , time. The Eight Hours in Mines Bill has been read a second time this week ; the Children Bill, which will !revolutionise and humanise the adm:nistration of the law where it touches the young —a measure which would have delighted the heart of Charles Dickens has got through Committee, and has brought upon the head of Mr. Herbert Samuel showers of congratu- lations for the able manner in which he has sustained the measure of his Chief and of his Department ; Mr. Birrell is expecting to get his Irish Universities Bill read a third time before the House rises; and the Licensing Bill is to be well started on its stormy course in Committee before the holiday arrives. So busy and memorable weeks are before the Parliamen- tary politicians; bat no week in this session will be more memorable than this one has been, because of one completed achievement of the Prime Minister, gr. Lloyd-George, and their colleagues. PENSION BILL THROUGEI THE COMUONS. As far as the House of Commons is concerned, the Old Age Pensions Bill is at length through ; its hard struggles in Committee and on Report of Committee stage are over, and the Third Reading will be taken before these lines are read. What will the Lords do with it ? They have had many an invitation from the critics of the measure in the House of Commons to maul the Bill or reject it on the plea that it ought to be a better Bill, such as the Conservatives have long been intending to bring in, only they made intention serve. A manifesto has been framed and circulated against it by some eminent men. But it is not likely that the Peers will be so venturesome as to stand between the poor and their old-age pensi ins. The Bill is really part of the Budget. It is a finance Bill in a very special sense, although it does also raise such important questions of national policy and national efficiency. The Lords, it may be assumed, will be glad of the Constitutional excuse not to damage the Bill, although making such speeches about it as will serve the electioneering purposes of the Opposi- tion. The Lords make up for their inability to inter- fere with elections in progress by electioneering in advance. But to do them justice they also give splendid electioneering material to the Ministerialists.

div.head: SLIDING SCALE SETTLEXIENT.
div.p: THE SLIDING SCALE SETTLEXIENT.

The Sliding Scale now stands in the Bill as the Government's compromise with those who wanted to save the Friendly Society pensioner. It was felt to be a hard case that a man whose superannuation, earned by his own thrift, was a little over ten shillings a week should have no claim on the State, while the man who had only saved six shillings a week would by five shilling= from the State be put into as good a position. It did not seem right that the workman who had only got nine shillings superannuation should have his Old Age money made up to fourteen shillings by the State, while the wofkman with eleven shillings superannuation got nothing more. The Sliding Scale remedies this inequality, but at the same time reduces the pension to these comparatively well-off old men. The five shillings is reserved for the very poor —the person of seventy with not more than eight shillings, so that the eight shillings will become thirteen. The; nine-shilings man will, however' be no worse off. He has the prospect of a pension of four shillings; and so on till the superannuation or savings reach twelve shillings. At that point the State pension is only one , shilling, and beyond that there is no pension. But ' for the difficulty of finding the money the Government would admit that this is even too symmetrical. The ideal thing would be to make the man who has , saved more than eight shillings not only as well off as I the eight shillings man, but to make him better off in proportion. So there was much pressure put upon the Government to adopt another scale under which a man would be sixpence better off for every shilling of his own saving above eight shillings. That is to say the saving of the eight shillings would mean thirteen shillings when the pension was added ; the saving of nine shillings would mean thirteen and six, and so on till the pension stopped at the man earning between fourteen and fifteen shillings a week. This appealed strongly to some of the supporters of the Government. But the Chancellor of the Exchequer with the respon- sibility for finding the money was obliged to be adamant, more especially as behind this claim was another, threatened by Mr. Keir Hardie, to restore the five-shilling pension to the man with ten shillings a week, and begin a sliding scale at that point. These good things must wait further Liberal economies.

THE POOR LW RELIEF DISQUA.LIFICITION.I The pauper disqualification is only operative until December 31st, 1910. Before that time, therefore, by the promised scheme of the Government amending the Poor Law, the aged pauper, who has only become a pauper since January Ist of this year, will be pro- I aided for in the same honourable way as those of his neighbours who have been fortunate enough to keep off the parish during the whole of this year. It amused those who have been watching the curious course of the Opposition on this Bill to notice a quick-change act on the Front Opposition Bench when the Government kept their word to Mr. Soares, the Member for Barnstaple, in accepting this amendment of their Bill. Previously, the Opposition had joined very warmly in the reproaches addressed to the Ministry concerning their treatment of the pauper. It was in vain that the Ministers reminded them that none of their own schemes had ever con. templated relieving the rates of the burden of th - existing paupers. Heartlessness was laid to their charge, and the House rang with the pathetic wails of Mr. Walter Long over the hard fate of the casual pauper in the agricultural districts. But now Mr Long resented the opportunity being passed on to him and his colleagues, if they should be in power in 1910. To be sure, that is a most unlikely contin- gency ; but the Government were freely accused of ' shunting their responsibilities on to the shoulders of their successors. Mr. Balfour tried to defeat the amendment on a question of order, and, when it was I ruled against him, lectured the Government on their " most flagitious way of dealing with the future obligations of time or of money." He actually voted against the amendment.

div.head: CHARACTER TEST.
div.p: THE CHARACTER TEST.

There was a final struggle on Tuesday night over the test of fitness to receive pensions. The Govern- ment have entirely redrafted their Bill in this respect, out of deference to criticism from the Labour Party, whose qualification to advise on a Bill like this is, of course, indisputable, and who have rendered invalu- able service. The only criticism to which they have laid themselves open is that of expecting more than it was quite reasonable to ask from a Government which was pledged to nothing more than to make a beginning. The Labour members were naturally apprehensive as to the construction which might he put on the bad behaviour disqualification. As the Bill was drafted, a man was to be disqualified if he had habitually refused to work, or habitually refrained from working when he was physically able to work, 'or if he had been brought into a position to apply for a pension through his own wilful act or misbehaviour. The Labour members saw danger in this clause, fearing its interpretation by the pension officer or by inquisitorial ponsion committees. The disqualification now is devoid of any such word as " misbehaviour." A man is to be disqualified only if he has failed to work according to his ability, opportunity, and need for the maintenance ,of himself and those legally dependent upon him. And as a guarantee against any inquiry. going too far back, or becoming too inquisitorial, it Is to be taken for granted that a man who has been a good member of a Friendly Society before sixty years of age does I not need to be held to account too strictly. Ile is not to be disqualified under this paragraph" if he has continuously for ten years up to attaining the age of I sixty, by means of payments to friendly, provident, or other societies or trade unions, or other approved steps, made such provision against old age, sickness nfirmity, or want or loss of employment as may bey iecognised as proper provison for the purpose b regulations under this Act."

* * - Still another definition or degree of drunkenness, this time from Otley. Superintendent Strain : If you were neither drunk nor sober, what condition were you in ? Prisoner : I was what you would call " lukewarm." Laughter). * * * It is an open question whether the local Conserva- tives did not get more entente copdiale, than was good for them. What with the travelling and the potency of tho " cordial " they got back from Paris very sleepy. Moreover, several had shrewd suspicions that they had dined off horse and snail pie under a clever disguise. * * * Few men have been in and out of the House of Commons so much as Lord Charles Beresford, who is now being talked of once again as a possible Parliamentary candidate. There always seems to be a constituency ready to take him, though he can never oblige any constituency for long. He was member for his native Waterford in Disraeli's last Administra- tion ; he sat for East Nlarylebone from 1335 to 134,9, having been ighting in Egypt in the interval ; from 1897 to 1900 he represented York. and he was mem- ber for Woolwich in 1902.

* * * The next election is apparently to be of the " big and little "type so far as political argument goes. We have already made the acquaintance of the big glass and the little glass of beer. The other evening at Southampton the Conservative Chief Whip, Sir Alexander Aeland-Hood made a reference to the Coal Hines (Eight flours) Bill, saying :—" The cry at the next election would not be the big and the little loaf, but the big coal-scuttle and the little one, and they should certainly use it." We have not the least doubt that they will " use " it—the last thing we should over accuse the Conservative organisers of would be any delicacy or hesitancy over the " use " they make of electioneering cries. People who put oat the notorious picture of the 4LI. loaf for GI. are not likely to boggle over a coal-scuttle.* Commander R. E. Peary has for the ninth time left New York for the frozen North. It is just three years this month since he started on his last journey, as a result of which sine months later —on April 21st, 1903—he planted the Stars and Stripes on an icy pinnacle only 174 nautical miles from the North Pole. No human beings had ever before reached so high a latitude —B7deg. 6rnin. N. —and by attaining it Peary beat Nansen's 1890 achievement by a degree all but eight minutes, and the record of the Duke of Abruzzi in 1900 by 33nain., or by 55 and 35 English miles respectively. Should he this time reach the Pole he will unfurl the American flag President Roosevelt has given him for the purpose. * * * A man may take good counsel, Ev'n from his foe.— Tennyson. He who calls in the aid of an equal understanding doubles his own. —Burke . You may have one grievance, but two are danger- ous, and three make you absurd.— Ba3sho.' Ingratitude is always a form of weakness. I have never known a man of real bility ungrateful. —Goethe. Noble souls, through dust and heat, Rise from disaster'and defeat The stronger.—Long f Oozy. The conditions of conquest are easy. We have but to toil awhile, endure awhile, believe always, anil never turn back.—R. L. Stevenson. The best man is the most unselfish man. Humble, constant, voluntary self-sacrifice—this is what con- stitutes the true dignity of math—Ain/el. Hopes of a settlement of the education question have not vet been abandoned. According to a London correspondent the chances of a compromise are not less than they were, and an influence little suspected has been operating in the cause of peace. The influence referred to is that of the „American and Colonial bishops who are now, or have been recently, in this country. Most of these bishops are familiar with systems of education under which undenomina- tional religious teaching is given, or which are purely secular. They have, it is stated, urged their English brethren with practical unanimity to come to an arrangement on the basis of the Government Educa- tion Bill. The views• must have considerably influenced the English bishops, and they will: strengthen the hands of the Archbishop of Canterburyl and others in their endeavours to effect a compromise which will be acceptable to moderate Churchmen, and ' which will give satisfaction to Nonconformists' opinion. *l* " Is Tolstay wholly sincere ? " is the question by a writer ia " Munsey's Magazine," and he goes on to say that the simplicity of the man is " hardly real. " His wife, who watches over him as tenderly as if lie had never declared marriage to be vile, sees to it that he is not deprived of creature comforts. Under his shaggy outer clothing he wears the finest linen. Though his food be simple, it is of the best, and is cooked with all the skill or a Parisian chef. Because of his old age he does not detect the kindly imposition that is practised on him. He says : "I am poor. I have scarcely a copeck. I can give nothing to charity." Literally, he speaks the truth ; but actually there is a fortune held by those whose pleasure it is to minister to his comfort He eats off the cheapest crockery, and says : "My food is as simple as any peasant's." He does not see that this food consists of daintily cooked viands, with peaches and other , fruit which many a rich banker could scarcely afford when out of season,

* * Within the last few days a considerable change, both of public and of military opinion, has taken place in regard to Mr. Haldane's Territorial Army. We no longer hear that the scheme is a failure, and some very competent authorities are now declaring that it is going to be a success. Of the 300,000 men required, 183,000 have already joined, and this, seeing that the new organisation has only been three months in existence, is considered extremely good. Ten thousand nem recruits were enlisted in the month of June, and if this goes on for a few months longer the whole number required will be forthcoming. The success of Mr. Haldane's great scheme will be received with satisfaction (says the London correspondent of the " Liverpool Post and Mercury ") by all except those who are in favour of compulsory service. The advo- cates of compulsory service have been from the first anxious to show that the scheme would fail, and they still continue to raise their croaking voices. It is clear, however, that their anticipations have been disappointed, and competent authorities like the military critic of the " Times " declare that Mr. Haldane's scheme is going to solve our military problem.

By the kind invitation of Mrs. Dodds a large number of the members of the Warrington Women's Suffrage Society were present at a garden party at Penketh House on Thursday afternoon. The previous day's rain had a beneficial effect on the garden, which was looking at its best, Mr. Dodds' roses being much admired. Tea was served in the house, and after- wards a meeting was held on the tennis lawn, Miss Massy (President of the Warrington Society) in the chair. A very able address was given by Miss Margaret Ashton, of Manchester, on " Woman's Suffrage." Mrs. Dodds proposed a vote of thanks to the speaker, Mrs. Parker seconded, and the vote was heartily accorded. Thanks were also tendered to Mrs. Dodds for her pleasant hospitality.

Manchester and District Bank. An ordinary meeting of the shareholders of the Nianchester and Liverpool District Banking Company, Ltd., will be held in Manchester on Friday next, when the following report of the directors will be presented: —" The Directors have to report that tho gross profit for the half year ending 30th June last, after providing for all bad and doubtful debts, is £298,655 11s. Bd., to which has to be added the amount brought forward from 31st December last, viz.: £50,703 11s. 7d. From this sum the following deductions have to be made : —Total expenses at the Head Office, London Office, and Branches, including salaries, stationery, taxes, &c, £110,851 14s. Id.; half-year's provision for income tax, £5,000 ; leaving a net profit of £233,513 12s. 2d. Tbe directors recommend the declaration of as dividerurof 21s. per share, which will take £165,900, leaving a balance of £67,613 12s. 2d. Of this it is proposed to carry to the Reserve Fund £lO,OOO • to Pension Fund £5,000, and to next account £52,613 12s. 2d. The Reserve Fund, with the above addition, will amount to £1,695,000. Mr. Andrew Bennie, having intimated to the Board that he desired to be relieved from the duties of Managing Director, retired from that position on the 30th ultimo. The Directors highly appreciate the services which Ur. Bennie has rendered to the Bank for many years, and are glad to announce that-lie will retain his seat on the Board. The Directors regret to intimate that Mr. Henry Davies, for many years a Director of the Lancaster Bank, and elected a director of this Bank in January last, died on May 9th. Daring the past half-year offices have been opened at Heaton Chapel and Knott End, Fleetwood, and a small sub-office at The Green, near I.liPom, Cumberland, has been closed. Offices have been opened since the close.ef the half- year at Birkdale, Buxton, Chester, and Colwyn Bay.

RAILWAYMEN'S PARADE.

I A combined church parade of St. Helens railwaymen was h'2ld on Sunday afternoon, on behalf of the Railwaymen's Orphanage, at the Parish Church. The procession was led by the Sutton-road Prize Band and there was a fair attendance, including Mr. R. Whistle— croft (L. and N.-W. stationmaster), Inspector Bonney, Messrs. J. Middlehurst, B. Skett (Garston), T. Oakes (G.C. stationmaster), T. Greases, A.E. Holt (secretary), and G. Travers (treasurer). The service was conducted by the Rev. Cyril Bardsley, vicar, who gave an address. "THINNER ALE "WANTED. A man who was charged at St. Helens came to the conclusion that since he got his head injured be was not fit to take any drink at all, or else the ale in St. must be too strong for him, and he would have to go and live somewhere where they sold " thinner "ale.— The Magistrate said it had taken the rnan a long time to come to the conclusion, for that was his sixty-third appearance before the court. He must go to gaol for twenty-eight days with hard labour.

THE VAGRANCY QUESTION. The Clerk brought before the Board the question of inter-county amalgamation on the question of vagrancy in Lancashire, Cheshire, Cumberland and Westmoreland. The matter had been under the consideration of a Joint Committee who now submitted a series of recommenda- tions, one of the chief being the provision of a mid-day meal for casuals whilst on tramp, at specified stations in the counties. The object was that there should be no excuse for begging on account of want of food. Mr. Hallows remarked that there would be more people roaming the country if they could come into the Workhouses for supper and breakfast and then have a mid-day meal somewhere else. There would not be anyone working soon. (Laughter.) Mr. Wright remarked that a mid-day meal of bread and cheese, such as was proposed, was not very much. The matter was deferred pendMg the receipt of further information.
APPOINTMENT.
The Clerk intimated that the Local Government Board had written confirming the appointment of Nurse Croughton at the Workhouse at a salary of £3O. FINANCE. _
Mr. Woodward reported total payments during the month of £1,783 13s. 2d. and a balance in the treasurer's hands of £2,138 Os. 11d. RUNCORN RURAL DISTRICT COUNCIL.

The fortnightly meeting of this Council was held at Dutton Workhouse on Tuesday, Mr. G. Pilling pre- siding. There were also present :—Messrs. T. Wright, S. Woodward, C. E. Linaker, 'l'. Baxter, J. Spruce, Admiral Jones-Parry, G. Egerton-Warburton, J. Hallows, J. B. Chadwick, A. Haining, J. H. Davies, E. Britcb, A. Broome, J. Bcoshavv, T. Guest, 11. Ala vrdsley, R. Nixon, W. Weir, G. Watson, G. div.p: THEiI HOSPITAL.

The Local Govern;iea-ifo-a-r-d-Wderting to the annual report of the medical officer of health, inquired if !the Council had considered the question of increasing the accommodation provided at the hospital. The letter was referred to the Isolation Hospital Committee. _

- -- The Isolation Hospital Committee accepted the tender of Mr. Billington for the painting of tbe outside of the building. It was reported that a modification of the plans for the erection of a porter's lodge would result in a saving of £l5O on the original amount, and it was decided to invite tenders for the building.

div.p: riiE 13 YEL A.W S.

The Chairman and Mr. Linaker were deputed to wait upon the Local Government Board with regard to the Counqil's byelaws which are being brought more up-to- date. The Board had written to the effect that in rural districts the byelaws should he drafted to meet the conditions in the separate townships.

div.head: DUST NUISA:NCE. . _ .
div.p: THE DUST NUISA:NCE. . _ .

Mr. Woodward said ik:e-p-ra-e-ti-o-e—o-f-Putting washings, sand and soil upon the roads in such hot weather and in such quantities as he had seen them put on recently, created dust to such an extent that it could be shovelled up. That,of course,meant a great nuisance to the residents. He suggested that pan scale, such as could be obtained from the United Alkali Company, should be used for the purpose. THE CLOSING OF SCHOOLS.

In his report Dr. Adams said there had been an out- break of whoopinr, cough and measles at Antrobus, but the schools would not be closed until the attendance fell below CO per cent. Mr. Woodward suggested that it would be a common serse procedure to close the schools for the summer holidays when an epidemic occurred at this time of the year. It was pointed out, however, that there would be difficulties in the wny of this course being adopted.

div.head: WESTON AFFAIRS.
div.p: WESTON AFFAIRS.

At a meeting of the Weston Parochial Committee, • Mr. Chadwick presiding, a letter from Costner Kelner Alkali Company, Ltd., was read, asking permission to • Jay gas and electric mains under the surface of South- road, Weston Point, to connect property belonging to them on the north side of the road with their works on , the south side of the road. The Committee recom- mended the Council to agree to this. A letter from • Mr. W. H. Jarvis, chief officer of the Castner Kelner , Fire Brigade, was read asking on behalf of certain resi- dents of the Parish if the Committee would favour the ' formation of a volunteer fire brigade for the parish. The Committee recommended that the necessary steps be taken to have the pressure of each of the hydrants in the Weston Ward tested ; and that Mr. Jarvis be thanked for his letter and informed of the action of the Committee. I The minutes were confirmed. A CONTRACTOR'S LOSS. Walton Inferior Sewerage Committee recommended that an allowance of £2O be made to Mr. Thomas Kilburn, the contractor for the sewerage scheme, , towards his losses on the contract. This was agreed to.

WORLD'S RECORD SWIM. Holbein swims 50 miles and breaks all records for the whole world. In this marvellous feat of endurance, Holbein relied upon " Ju-Vis" to maintain his strength and he seemed quite unfatigued at the end of this marvellous swim. Mr. liolhein was in the water 13 hours, 47 minutes.

div.head: RUNCORN AND WIDNES.
div.p: RUNCORN AND WIDNES.

WIDNES CAPTAIN DROWNED. Joseph Rotherham, residing in Widnes-road, Widnes, and captain of the flat Excelsior, whilst going out with the tide on Monday, was knocked off the fiat by the tiller, near Hale Head, and drowned. The body was afterwards recovered. TOO MANY GLASSES.

At Widnes on .Uonday morning, Annie Jones an old offender, of no fixed abode, was charged with being drunk and disorderly on Friday afternoon, and with breaking the plate-glass windows of the Baths Spring Vaults and doing damage to the extent of £4.— Prisoner pleaded guilty, end was seat to goal for three months.

div.head: EARLESTOWN AND NEWTON.
div.p: EARLESTOWN AND NEWTON.
EARLESTOA'N MAN FOUND DROWNED.

' On Sunday afternoon the body of a man was taken from the St. Helens Cant], opposite Tinker's Soapworks, St. Helens. It was later identified as that of Patrick Beay, about fifty-sis, a sugar works labourer, of Earles- town, whose brother lives in ‘Vaterloo-place,St.Helens. It is understood that some weeks ago the man left. work and went to see some relatives in Ireland. How he got into the canal is a mystery. The inquest was held at St. Helens on Tuesday night. Evidence was given that the deceased was a labourer, who had worked at the Earlesto wn Sugar Works, but five weeks ago he visited his brother at Roscommon, Ireland. He returned on June 27, and from that time stayed at various lodging-houses and drank rather heavily. On Saturday last he was seen leaning over the rails by the side of the canal near the place where his body was found. A verdict of" Found drowned " was returned.

div.head: WOMAN AND A HAMMER. SERIOUS ASSAULT ON A HUSBAND AT EAR LESTOWN.
div.p: WOMAN AND A HAMMER. SERIOUS ASSAULT ON A HUSBAND AT EAR LESTOWN.

At the Newton-le-Willows Police Court, on Thursday morning, Agnes Barrett, of North-street, Earlestown, was charged with assaulting her husband, John Barrett, on June 27th. The charge had been reduced to common assault from one of unlawfully and maliciously wound- ing. She pleaded not guilty.—The husband stated that he went to sleep on the sofa in the parlour, when be was suddenly wakened by a blow on the head. He was getting up to see what was the matter, when he received another violent blow. He turned and saw his wife leaving the room with a hammer in her hand.— Prisoner's daughter said she saw her mother go into the parlour with a hammer in her hand, and a girl named Elizabeth Pickthorn, who was in the house at the time, said she heard a noise like a blow being struck.—A police-constable stated he found the hammer in the front garden with blood stains upon it.—Mr. J. W. Knowles, for the defence, said there was no evidence to show that prisoner com- mitted the assault, and that the husband was struck with a hammer at all. On the very morning of the alleged assault prisoner was assaulted by her husband. It was very simple for the husband to rub blood on the hammer and put it in the garden in order to accuse his wife.—Prisoner was fined £5 and given a month in time to pay. In default of payment the term was one month's imprisonment.

NEWPON U RBAN COUNCIL. The monthly meeting of the above Council was held at Earlestown Town Hall on Monday evening, under the presidency of Mr. T. Ormand. The other members present were Messrs. W. Thompson, T. Ritchie, L. E. Pilkington, G. F. Clarke, J. Naylor, E. L. Bent, C. B. F. Borron, J. Higharn and C. Cole (clerk), R. T. Surtees (water engineer) and A. Bowes (surveyor.) PROPOSED OPEN RATTLING PLACE. At a meeting of the Water Committee, on June 15th, reference was made to the proposed use of the cooling , pond at the pumping station as an open bathing place. The Clerk reported upon the provisions of the Baths and Wash-houses Acts, 18IG to 1809, which, he stated, 'would need adopting by the Council. Ho also sub- mitted draft by-laws for the management, use, and regulation of the bathing place. ' It was resolved that the Council, at its next meeting, be recommended to adopt the Baths and Washhouses Acts, 184 G to 1899, for the district of Newton-in- Makerfield. _ _ _

It was also resolved that a special Baths Committee be appointed and that Councillors Ormand, Borron Collingwood, Evans, Ritchie, Seton and Tunstall be; the members thereof, and that the draft by-laws be referred to them for consideration. _

It was further resolved that the Water Engineer be directed to obtain tenders for the wood fencing and a portion of tho other work required for adapting the cooling pond for use as a bathing place, and that such tenders when received, be, with the view of expediting the matter, referred to the Chairman and Engineer, with power of acceptance and of ordering the whole of the work to be proceeded with. The minutes of the committee were approvedr' BRIDGE-STREET BRIDGE.

At a meeting of the 'Highways Committee, the Surveyor, as directed at the last meeting, reported as to the possibility of improving the bridge in Bridge-street and submitted plan of a new bridge floor composed of steel troughtng which could be carried out without disturbing the existing parapet walls and would lower the level of the crown of the bridge and thus improve the gradients. It was resolved that the further consideration of the report be deferred until the next meeting.

roLtAmoN OF NEWTON LAKE AND MILLINGFORD BROOK. With reference to the pollution of Newton Lake and Millingford Brook, the Clerk and the Medical Officer of Health reported, at a special meeting of the Sanitary Committee on June sth as to the action taken since that. time the Haydock Council had provided sewage treat- ment works by which the stream' called Ellam's Brook, where it entered this district, had been rendered appar- ently free front sewage pollution. As regarded the recent pollution of Millingford Brook, the Inspector of Nuis- ances reported that on Tuesday last the County Medical officer of Health inspected the lake and also the brook, on which inspection he accompanied Dr. Sergeant, and gave his opinion of the state of the brook at various points. He also reported as to the apparent pollution of the brook at Ashton-in-Makerfield, where it appeared that sewage had recently been allowed to discharge from a sewer and to flow into the brook. It was resolved that the Clerk be instructed to call the attention of the Golborne and Ashton Urban Dis- trict Councils to the pollution ; that Dr. Sergeant's suggestion as to the cleaning out of that part of the lake which is entered by Millingford Brook be com- municated to Lord Newton's agent ; and that the matter be again considered at the next meeting of the committee. The minutes were passed

div.head: WARRINGTON TOWN COUNCIL. ADVERTISING THE TOWN.
div.p: WARRINGTON TOWN COUNCIL. ADVERTISING THE TOWN.
Alderman Bennett's Word of Warning. THZ PROPOSZD FOOTERINZ AT HOWLEY.

The monthly meeting of the Warrington Town Council was held at the Town Hall on Tuesday evening. At the outset Alderman Pierpoint was elected to the chair, as the Mayor had not returned from Stockport where he had been attending the opening of the new Town Hall by the Prince of Wales. Later his Worship ari iced and presided oNor the remainder of the proceed- ings. There were also present :—Aldermen A. Bennett, L.Ellison, John Evans ; Councillors J.Ball,T. Barton, J. Broadhurst, T. Chantler, J. Dickenson, James Evans, J. Hawthorn, 3. T. Locker J. Lord, 3. Pemberton, W. Rogers, J. Sankey, H. Locker, J. Skelland, T. S. Steel, J. Fulton-Smith, J. Wilkinson, W. J. Wilson; Messrs. J. L. Whittle (town clerk), A. T. Hallaway (Deputy town clerk), J. Fairhurst (borough treasurer), T. Longdin (borough smveyor), J. Dens (water engineer), \V. S. Haddock (gas engineer), F. V. L. Mathias (electrical ennineer), J. H. Murray (director of eiecation) aud Dr. J. C. Hibbert (medical officer). THE OLD WARPS ESTATE. Alderman ELLISON moved "That the control and management of the Old Warps Estate be vested in the Town Hall, Parks and Baths Committee." Alderman BENNETT, in seconding, said he was quite sure this was a right policy, because the magnificent estate would be in the hands of the committee best qualified to deal with it. Hitherto they had not made anything like the use of the land that they ought to have made of it. The resolution was passed. ADVERTISING THE TOWN. COMMITTEE TO BE FORMED. Councillor PEMBERTON moved :—(1) That a COS- roittea be appointed, called the "Towns Committee." (2) That a sum of £3) be granted to the Towns Com- mittee forthwith. fie said the intention was that the Towns Committee should bring before the notice of the people interested the advantages Warrington possessed for works and manufactories. .Without boasting, he did not think there was a town in England so advantage- ' ously situated for works. There were six railways, two barge canals, and an ocean practically at their door. The Corporation provided electricity, gas, water, and , eeerything a manufacturer wanted. There CVIS land waiting to be developed, and there was not the ' sliehtest doubt the Patents Act had brought several works to kleglanl and would bring more. if they could induce works to come Warrington, it would reduce the rates and make more profits for the electricity and water departments. o,ber towns did a similar thing. He was informed that St. Helens only at their last Council meeting discussed this question, and a resolution was passed that, if the Council could legally do so, they should appoint an agent to get into touch with firms on the Continent to bring their works to St. Helens. The position of Warrington was far superior to that of St. Helens and its facilities were , greater. Probably a score of towns in England spent a lot of money in advertising thernselvgs as pleasure resorts, and thus benefiting the ratepayers; and he did not see why Warrington should not assist the tow and inhabitants in a somewhat similar way. Councillor EVANS, in seconding, said the matter was a very important one, hut he thought Councillor Pemberton should have said something about the rating of new works that might come into the town. He saw no reason why large works should not receive some con- sideration, as much as portions of villages and proper- ties near the borough boundary when they were taken into a borough. (neer, bear.) Alderman BENNETT said he was in general sympathy with the idea, although he sometimes wondered why they were always anxious to make these tremendous towns. His own observations bad led him to believe that very often, while they had been increasing in wealth and prosperity, in every other i espect they had been deteriorating. The growth of a town to these abnormal dimensions was not necessarily a benefit. (Hear, hear.) He did not oppose the idea of Councillor Pemberton, because he was a member of the committee which made some preliminary investigation with a view to carrying out the object in view, but they did not want to set before them the merw idea of bigness and mere industrial prosperity. It was possible to pursue that idea until the town became a huge Widnes or a bigger St. Helens. If they were going to devoe on those lines he would rather have less prosperity and a -somewhat pleasinter town in which to live. If they carried out the idea Councillor Pemberton had ie view they should see that they planned out their operations on some statesmanlike and roll-considered plan. The works should ho pet down on proper lines and a minimum requirement should be that they should con- sume their own smoke. Don't let them for the sake of an enormous increase of wealth, sending up the value of land and filling the pockete of a few investors, spoil the appearance of the town. The TOWN CLER K : Chemical works. (Laughter.) Alderman BENN ETV stid that that was a matter that was in, his mind. They did not want deleterious industries which, for the sake of making wealth,created a great deal of discomfort. Councillor FELTON-SM ITII said that, without detract- ing from anything which had been said by Councillor Pemberton, he should like to call attention to the fact that a committee was apnointed some time ago to act somewhat on the same lines as those suggested that evening. Was it in order that that committee should be dissolved so that the new an egested committee could act? Councillor Evass : That was an advertising committee. The CHAIRMAN : That ended with the municipal year. The now committee will not clash with any

existing committee. Councillor PEMBERTON said with regard to the ques- tion of rating it W,s a detail for the new committee to go into. With raference to Alderman Bennett, what he feared was a matter for the committee, to a great extent, who would be under the control of the Council. What they wished to do was to flad work for an ever- growing population. If the woas did not grow and the people did not find work, they had to go to other towns where there was prosperity. Warrington had as much right to grow as any other town. He wished to remind the Council that there was a Town Planning Bill before Parliament and that would give therm potter to say what they would have and where they would have it. As to the smoke nuisance, manufacturers all over the country were doing all they could do to abate it, in their own interests. The resolution was then agreed to.

HONOUR FOR VIE BOROUGH TREASURER. Alderman BENNETT in moving the confirmation of the minutes of the Finance and Estate Committee alluded to the fact that the Borough Treasurer had I been attending the annual conference of the Institute, of Borough Treasurers and that it bad done him the honour to make him a member of the Council. There were six Trembers of the Council for the whole of England and ex-officio members. That was a compli- ment to Mr. Fairhurst, as well as to the Council. (Hear, hear). Councillor WILKINSON seconded, and the motion was carried. MESSRS. MILLING'S SICY SIGN. The To erg CLERK at a meeting of the Street Improvement Committee reported that Messrs. Henry Milling and Company, Limited, had erected a sky sign der their premises in Horsemarlcet-street contrary to the Warrington Corporation Act of 1523. It was resolved that no sky sign be allowed in the berough,and that Messrs. Milling he served with notice to remove the sign erected by them. Alderman Br NNErr moved the confirmation of the minutes of the committee except that relating to sky signs, which he wished to withdraw for the moment, because the matter was still under consideration. The committee did not deviate from their intention not to allow the town to he disfigured by the wholesale erection of sky signs, but this was a special case and was under special consideration and the matter would be brought before the Council in some other shape. Councillor EVANS seconded, and the minutes were parsed with the exception named. THE GEOROE SHEFFIELD EXHIBMON. _ .„

*At a meeting of the :‘lnseum Committee it was reported that 7,G-1O visits had been paid to the exhibition during the four weeks it. was open, and It was resolved that the best thanks of the committee be tendered to Messrs. Birtles, Mawson and Whittle for their assist- ance in regard to the exhibition. Alderman BENNET I', in moving the confirmation of the minutes, alluded to the number of visitors, and said the exhibition was a tribute to the memory of a well- known Warrington artist, as well as an admirable means of advertising the institution. They hoped to have a permanent memorial of the late Mr. Sheffield by possess- ing one of his beautiful pictures to adorn the permanent collection. (Hear, hear.) Alderman ELLISON seconded, and the motion was carried.

A BATHS INNOVATION. SWIMMING TO BE TAUGHT. At a meeting of the Town Hall, Parks and Baths Committee it was decided that the bath-keeper be allowed to teach swimming between the hours of 7 and S a.m. and 2 to 3 p.m. each day of the week except Saturday, and that the following charges be made, the bath-keeper to receive 50 per cent. thereof :—Gentle- men, twelve lessons (including season ticket, 12s. 63.,) LI Bs.• single lesson (including admission to bath), 2s. Boys (under 10 years of age), twelve lessons (including season ticket, 7s. 6d.), £1 ; single lesson (including admission to bath), Is. 61 School boys, a class of not less than ten in number on Wednesday afternoons •, Ach pupil per lesson.- (including admission to bath) Is. 6d. The CHAIRMAN moved the confirmation of the minutes. The motion was seconded by Alderman ELLIt,ON and carried.

div.head: LIVERPOOL CORPORATION BILL.
div.p: LIVERPOOL CORPORATION BILL.
--- The TOWN CLERK, at a meeting of the, Water Com- mittee, reported that the opposition of the Corporation

Alde,man-PlF.Reemr seconded. Alderman B ESNE 17 said a footbridge would be an advantage, but he did not think they were pursuing a very boll or sagacious policy. Ten years ago they had i a much larger scheme n mind for carrying not only foot passengers, hut vehicular trail. They also had a plan for deag ng comprehensively with Bridge root and the making of bridges at the Wilderspool crossings and across Arpley Meadaws. He was not opposing the present sehe:ne though he doubted whether they were acting with real econorny. A proper bridge at Howley would result in the erection of so much new property that the increased ratable value would be suffizient to wipe out the cost.fle could not help thinking they had missed a good opportunity of dealing with Wilderspool cross- ings in conjunction with the bridge the London and North-Western Railway Company were putting-over the Mersey. However, when he mentioned the matter he was met with the bogey of the rates. The sum of £6OO seemed to be a ridiculously small amount to spend on a bridge, and be hoped even for a tempo:- try bridge they were not going to have an abortion. He did not think it fair to ask the Borough Surveyor to undertake the preparation of plans—it was not his work—and they ought to employ expert knowledge to deal with such an important scheme. The Town Clerk sent for a catalogue containing an illustration of the proposed bridge. Alderman Brsserr said they appeared to be getting an ironmong, r's catalogue and buying a bridge as they would a watering can. (Langbter )

• Alderman PtEuroterr It is an art brio*. catalogns. Alderman PfeePoreaT said Alderman Bennett seemed to speak somewhat against the new bridge in one breath and in another breath he was abaelutely in favour of it. The Bridge Foot question had been proposed and advo- cated for a long time, but it had been opposed first of all by people who were interested in the river, and who wished to conserve or enlarge their own interests as against what be considered to be the interests' of the town. It was a question of cantilevers or a new bridge, and cantilwers lost, so they would have to make a new bridae. Perhaps it was the bast thine, but it WAS a qeeetion of utility with him (Alderman Pierpoint). He thought it absolutely necessary to have a vehicular bridge connecting Latchford end Fairfield wards and so open out Victoria Park, but they had been driven into the position of having to drop the vehicular bridge in favour of a foot bridge. The town could not possibly afford the luxury of d new bridge, and the way out of the difflentty was a footbridge. Latchford Ward,which was one of the largest ivards in the town, was being tbic'ily covered with cottages and many men who resided there and worked at Rylands' Bros. would be saved is considerable walk by Warrington Bridge when the foot bridge was made. He wished Alderman Bennett. instead of damning them with faint praise, would give the committee credit for having the beat intent iana anti a little common sense. Councillor Bear, thought they ought to have some- thing better than a font bridge. Alderman Bennett was afraid of cunpnsing the scheme because he might get nothing at all. He (Councillor B all)qnite sympathised with the Alderman's attitude with regard to Warrington Bridge. The town was growing rapidly and even if they had a new bridge for vehicular traffic for crossing Howley or Arplev Meadows they would soon require a new bridge at Bridge Foot. They were only postponing the evil day, and the cost which, he thought, would increase as time went on. Every time he passed over Warrington Bridge he felt almost ashamed that a town of such magnitude and prmptmts should be content to have such a miserable structure. The bridge and the road were bail and the whole question required careful consid-tration. He felt sure the bulk of the ratepayers would be gr•ttifiecl by the erection of a new bridge and not with a small, inconvenient and inadequate alteration by way of cantilevers or anything similar. Councillor PEMBERTON said he understood that the Borough Surveyor was simply to prepare plans, not that the work should be proceeded with. He was in favour of the bridge if perambulators and bicycles could he pushed over it. The plan stowed steps on one side of the bridge. He understood the plan was to come before the Council again. The Tows Camera : It will come before yon again. Connoillor PEMBERTON said a vehicular bridge at , Howley was not necessary. If they spent £20,000 on a bridge they would get the train° from Manchester to Lymrn and other places, but they would get no further. Until they got a main road over that part of the town they would have a bridge going to nowhere. The rate- payers were not anxious that more money should be spent. They were arxious that economy consistent I with efficiency should be exercised. He was sure Alderman Bennett would be pleased when be saw the bridge, which would be only temporary. I Councillor SINGLETON said he was in farmer of a footbridge as he did not think the time was opportune for the erection of a structure to carry vehicular traffic. Councillor STEEL wished to know whether the Conn- cil would have an opportunity of considering the plan on a future occasion. He understood there were to be steps on one side of the bridge. The Tows CLERK : We shall consider that question. Conncillor STEEL said that if what was proposed was the best they could get he was in favour of it, as he thought it was time they had a bridge from Howley Ward to Latchford Ward. Ile hoped that when the. plan came up for consideration they would he able to arrange to get over the bridge without the difficulty of steps. The bridge should be so arranged that people would be able to take perambulators over it. (Ilear, hear.) I The TOWN Carnra : If we can secure the land we shall dispense with steps. The MAYOR, in replying, said he was surprised to hear Alderman Bennett's speech. No committee could have been more whole-hearted in considering the bridge question. He wished to remind him that the rates were now 7s. 83, in the £, and that if they carried out his idea they would be increased to 12s. They would require to spend RP20,003 on bridges, and what would the ratepayers and the manufacturers do ? (A Voice : " Shut up.") They could see no prospect of putting up expensive bridges, and he understood that not only could a footbridge be obtained for .C6OO, but that it was possible the um of £450 allowed -for the Howley Recreation Ground might be dev.- ted to the cost of the erection of the new structure. (Hear, hear.) They had Isome aWkward people to deal with, and if they built the bridge in some part of the river the cost would be , not £6OO but a few thousands. They did not want to I go to law ; they had had enough of it. The minutes were then agreed to. it WELSHMAN'S PRAISE,

At the Borough Police Court, on Saturday, the Chief Constable said it was very complimentary to the public of Warrington that there was no rea cause of drunkenness or disorder arising out -of the Walking Day celebrations. The people generally behaved thenrelves remarkably well. Accident to a Warrington Volunteer. On Saturday Private G. Knight, of the 4th Battalion, met with an accident at Altcar Range. He was con- veying a message to another part of the field, and while passing another volunteer who was having some shooting practice the rifle he was using exploded, and Knight was injured in the thigh and leg, no one else being hurt. He was conveyed to the Warrington Infirmary for treatment, and is reported to be doing well. Alleged Lead Thef t at Winwick. Mr. Herbert Turley Chapman, aged thirty-eight, assistant surveyor to the Lancashire County Council, has been appointed county.surveyor for Somersetshire, ' at a salary of £5OO, with £250 for travelling expenses and £2OO for office expenses. There were 114, applicants for the position Mr. Chapman has been successively assistant to the county surveyor of West Sussex, district surveyor of maia reads and bridges in Derbyshire, nd for the last ten years under the Lancashire County Council. Theft of Fish. At the Warring,ton Borough Court, on Thursday, a boy and girl named James and Fanny Cooper, 10, Stoney-yard, pleaded guilty to stealing 31b. of fish, of the vale of Is. 31., from a box at the stall of William Whittaker in the Fish Market on Wednesnay night. The Chief Constable stated that Police-constable Vast saw the defendants in Horsemarket-street with the fish in a bag, which they admitted having stolen from the market. The boy was ordered to receive six strokes with the birch rod, and the girl was fined 103. Still unsurpassed, Puns lER CYCLRS at 6 guineas. —Agent, .7: S. P.S.A. Meeting. At the meeting of the Wycliffe P.S.A. on Sunday the Secretary (Hr. B. Farrar) presided. Owing to the holidays, there was- only a smallsattendance. The Secretory spoke upon "The observable changes around us, the unchangeable God and His Word" Mr. William Light gave the address upon "Thou hast made man a little lower than the angels." The lessons drawn were that God is seen in the smaller things around us es well as in the greater, and that He is also beard and felt in the lower experiences of life as well as in the greater. God is seen, heard and felt in the smaller sanctuary, as well as in the Cathedral. BABY CARRIAGES of every description.—J. S. GARLAND, 51 to 55,Bridge st.,Warrington.—Advt. Liverpool Wesley Guild Council. . Under the auspices of the newly-formed Liverpool Wesley Guild Council, of which the Rev. A. E. Sharpley, of Bootle, is the president, the first annual garden party was held at Valley Field Farm, Aigburth, an ideal spot for such gatherings, on Saturday after- noon. The Council embraces the young people's societies in connection with the Wesleyan Churches in Liverpool and the surrounding districts, and there were about 450 members of the guilds present f,rom Liverpool, West Derby, Warrington, St. Helens, South- port, Prescot, Widnes, Gersten (Banks-road), Bootle, Birkenhead and Wirral: The proceedings opened with a reception, which was followed by a number of selections by the Tranrnere Silver Gleam Prize Band, games and sports. The Bootle County-road Guild gave an open-air concert on the lawn attached to the farm.—A public meeting was afterwards .11,31 d the Rev. J. Wesley Hart (district secretary), presiding, in the absence of Mr. H. G. Hough (treasurer) ; aad the, Rev. Arthur Myers, of Linaci e, gave an appropriate address upon the principles of Methodism, and, urged all present to do their utmost for them. The New Union Clerk. An interesting ceremony took place in the Board- room of the Salford Union last week, when Mr. Arthur Bottotnley, who recently resigned the office of First Assistant Clerk to the Guardians,' to take up the post of Cloak to the Guardians of the Warrington Union, was the recipient of a handsome 15 carat gold albert, subsctibed for by the officers of the Union. In making the presentation on behalf of himself and the officers of the Union, Mr. Townson, the clerk to the Guardians, paid tribute to the conspicuous ability dis- played by Mr. Bottornley during the eight years he had been at Salford, and explessed his regret at ; losing one from whom he had always received the I utmost loyalty and assistance, but at the same time congratulated him on the occasion of his appointment to the higher position of Clerk to the Warrington ' Board. He trusted that Mr. awl Mrs. Bottomley and family would be given the best' of health and every I happiness, and that the step which Mr. Bottomley was now taking would only be one leading to still higher , things.—The Rev. J. Dyer Bray (Nonconformist Instructor), Mr. Jenkinson (Relieving Officer), Dr. o,an (District Medical Officer) and Mr. IL Hulme (Settlement Officer) all joined in wishing success to ' Mr. Bottomley in his new sphere of labour and referred in affectionate terms to the good relations which had always existed between Mr. Bottomley, themselves, and all the other officers of the Union. Mr. Bottomley replied, and after thanking the officers for the very handsome chain they had given him, I referred, in feeling terms, to his severance from them• and the associations of the Salford Union, , and he expressed the hope that he might find the officers of the Warrington Union such firm and lasting friends and such hearty co-operators as he had found those of the Salford Union to be. He hoped his successor, Hr. Inchley, would be as happy and as comfortable (and he felt sure he would be) at Salford as he had been.

the Jew as you treat the Christian, nor the Catholic as the Protestant. Mr. Birrell tried to meet this difficulty by "facilities." But the practical educational objections to facilities are scr great that no one who knows much about the internal working of schools would advocate this method. Ur. McKenna resorted to " contracting out," but this, from the educational "'Ant of view, ie even worse. We must recognize the fact that different people , .wish for different kinds of religious teaching of their ! children, and only by satisfying this can we arrive at a permanent agreement. It must be" all " or "none." The great majority of the nation votes against "n me." I Let us have " all." But ought denominational teaching to be paid for out of the rates? Why not? If one , form of religious teaching (Cowper Temple) may be paid for out of the rates, why not another? Da we n)t all pay ' rates —Jews, Christians, Catholics and Protestants ? If all contribute, may not all share? " But,'''say others, " we admit that this is just and fair, but we contend-that it is not practicable." Let us see. First, we mint recognize that the I problem in the town is distinct from that in the village. I We must c .nsider them separately. In the town the I matter is comparatively simple. Let every school in the town be under the dantrol and manage.Ment of the ' Local Education Authority Let it be the duty of the

t non ty. .aty (.4 . Authority to ascertain by means of a Creed Register the numbers of children belonging to the different religious bodies. Then let the Authority allocate the schools in proportion to the numbers of the different denominations, FO that in one school Church of England teaching is given,in another Roman Catholic,in a third Wesleyan, and so on. The schools should be So arranged that a child may find within a reasonable distance of his home a school of the denomination to which he belongs. The difficulty (a 1 tests for teachers would vanish by this plan, as teachers appointed by the Local Education Authority would be placed in the ' school where the teaching• was in accordance with their own religious belief. Popular control would also be secured. The common objection to this plan is that it is impossible to provide denominational teach- ing fur every denomination. This, of course, is true. Nor can this be secured by any plan whatsoever. The wishes, however, of the /peat majority would be met by providing for the principal denominations, and the principles of a very small minority would have to be ' safeguarded by a conscience clause. We now turn to the more difficult problem of the single school areas. It is obvious that, with the exception of certain places, where the ' people arfi all of one mind, it is impossible ; to please every one. All that we can do I is to ask what is the plan which is most just and fir to all. I would propose that the religious teaching given in the school be that which is in accordance with the belief of the majority, whatever that belief, may be. The Head Teacher should also be of the same belief. Where there is a second teacher, he I should be-appointed to teach the minority, and where there is but one teacher, an outside teacher should be I allowed to give instruction to the minority. Let us suppose that in a given place there is a Church of England school, bat the majority I of the people are Wesleyans. Then let the head I teacher be a Wesleyan and let him give Wesleyan instruction, and, if there be no second teacher, let ; the clergyman of the parish teach the Church children. ! I believe that this plan would woi k justly. But, above all, let us put aside the effort to win ,a victory for our own body, and let us base our policy I upon fairness and equity. Thus only can we bring about a permxnent settlement of a question which has been too long unsettled.

MILITARY FUNERAL AT WARRINGTON. ,

The funeral of the late Mr. Christopher Plunkett, I Orford-lane, master tailor at Orford Barracks, took ' place, with full military honours, at the Warrington Cemetery on Tuesday afternoon. The deceased had been in indifferent health for some time. but latterly had much improved, the end coming somewhat suddenly. He had bad a long and creditable military career. He enlisted in the old 47th Regiment in 1866, transferring some years later to the flrst Bth Regiment ,as sergeant master tailor. He retired on pension in 1890. He afterwards acted as canteen manager to his old regiment for some time, and later took up the appointment of master tailor to the Bth and 40th Regimental Districts at Warrington, continuing to hold the position to the , time of his death. Deeerieed was very well known in I Warrington, and the funeral was attended by a large number of civilian friends, in addition to the whole of the troops at the Barracks. All the offfcers of the combined depots were present, ;as well as the sergeants, many of whom came specially from Altcar Camp. They were headed by Major Edridge, Major Bundock, Captain Howard Vyse, Lieutenants G rounde, Marshall and H utchinson,Q ua rter- masters Bayley and Baines, and Sergeant-Majors Del:nage, Burnett, Jones, Lee and Atkinson. The ser- vice at the graveside was conducted by the Rev. James Davies, assisted by the Rev. IL Russell. The ceremony ; was a most impressive one, the band of the depot coming specially from Altear camp in order to take I part. After the playing of the hymn " Days and ! moments quickly flying," three volleys were fired over the grave and the" Last Post" was sounded. The deceased was a member of No. 118 "Lodge of Lights" of Freemasons and the following brethren were present :—Bros. John Rogerson. div.head: WIRRAL SHOW.
div.p: WIRRAL SHOW.

Cattle breeders who have entered specimens of their stock for the Wirral and Birkenhead Agricultural Show will be gratified to hear that they will have as a rival competitor no less a personage than King Edward. This is the first occasion in the history of the society that his Majesty has figured in the list of esbfbitors. Apart from the added attractiveness which it gives to the show, the Royal compliment is appreciated by the council of the society as a pleasing manifestation of the generous interest which the Sovereign takes in agricultural affairs, and as a flattering proof of the important rank which the Birkenhead Shc.w now occu- pies amongst the great agricultural shows of the kingdom.

div.head: "POCKET WIRELESS."
div.p: "POCKET WIRELESS."

Telepathy, or thought transference, is to develop new possibilities. Electric currents change the surface tension of mercury, cauh- ing it to rise and fall in a vertical capiilary tube, and it appears that this effect is mag- nified and utilised in an exceedingly sensi- tive receiver. This device may detect such delicate impulses as those sent from 'a con- cealed pocket battery. It would seem that this miniature wireless might have other uses, but this inventor's suggestion is that, with a battery in his pocket, a confederate, favourably placed in the body of a hall,, would be able to send messages to a mind reader on the platform without anybody knowing it.

div.head: WHEN CORN ETATS UNDER WATER.
div.p: WHEN CORN ETATS UNDER WATER.

Cork, in spite of its buoyancy, will not rise to the surface again from a depth of 200 feet below the ocean's surface, owing to the great pressure of water. At any depth short of that it will gradually work its way back to the surface.

div.head: MUSIC FROM SAND.
div.p: MUSIC FROM SAND.

It is said that sand will, under pressure, emit sounds of distinct musical value. If a quantity of sand be put into a xessel, and submitted to pressure by friction between the grains, sounds are produced which some- times resemble a chirp. The finer the grain, the higher is the pitch of the note sounaed.

div.head: MELTING OF ICE.
div.p: MELTING OF ICE.

Skaters may frequently have n9ticed twigs, brown leaves, and straw sunk mans inches in ice, and wondered bow they got there. Being ready absorbers of heat, these fragments of vegetation have become warm in the sun's rays and slowly sunk into the little icy graves of their own making. IMPRISONS THE HEAT. The atmosphere of the earth 'acts very much in the same way as does the glass of a greenhouse—it allows the rays of the sun to pass through, but imprisons the heat. Thus it is colder on the top of a mountain than at the sea level, because, though the mountain- top is nearer the sun, the atmosphere is very much less dense.

div.head: EXPERIMENT WITH SHADES.
div.p: EXPERIMENT WITH SHADES.

The eyes of an average person are capable of dietinguishing about 25 different shades between black and white. An enthusiastic scientist employed no less than 200 shades in an experiment which led Jilin to this conclu- sion; but the great majority of these were too near, alike to be distinguished by the eye. These were not shades of different colours, but simply grey surfaces passing gradually from white to black.

div.p: 1,200 Pus To THE MINUTE. }

Puff, puff, puff! The train was just leav- ing the station, and the puffs of the locomo- tive, at first slow, grew faster and faster, and finally seemed to cease in the roar of the train. "It is the emission of the waste steam through the chimney that causes that puffing sound," said an engine-driver. "As the train gathers speed the puffs increase in rapidity, and when ten a second are emitted the ear can't distinguish them separately any longer—it hears them as a continuous roar. The majority of people, on this account, think a locomotive only puffs at starting. Really, she puffs all the time, only the puffs are too rapid to be recognisable. A train going a mile a minute gives twenty puffs to the second."
