A gentleman was passing up the street of ons of our great cities, when he noticed a poor little street arab, wh.o, judging from his pinched features, was suffering severely from exposure.

'Where is your coat?" he kindly asked. "Not got _one," the little chap answered, carelessly, though he shivered. "But you will be frozen. Who iss your mother, child?" "Not got one," he replied again. "Well, where de• you live?—what home have you?" , "Not got one, he repeated, in. the same matter-Of fact way. "You poor little soul!" the gentleman ex- claimed; "whet have you got?" To his astonishment, the boy's whole manner changed, and he said, with proud content: "Why, I have got a father! Things is a bit rough just now, because he is in hospital; but he will pull through, I am not afraid—father is all as I want." The reply went hOme.to the heart of the gentleman, who had been a trifle despondekt The lad had helped him to realiee that he, too, had a Father—in Heaven. JANE ELLN HAnGREAVBS.
CATCHING PRAWNS. All among the slippery rocks, Wetting shoes, and spoiling frocks, See May and Fred, and little Flo! Net in hand, they cunning look In each seaweed-hidden nook,

And watch the prawns dart to and fro. "Catch them—catch them, quick!" cries May, "Hold the net down, that's the -way, Just as the fisherman would do." In the water, Fred, knee-deep, Sinks his net and makes a sweep, And some are caught and some leap through. "Will they bite me?" falters Flo. Braver May replies, "Oh, no! Now, hold the basket, that's the thing! Shut the lid, or out again They'll jump back, and what would Jane Say if no supper home we bring?"

The prawns they swim, the prawns they le4p, But suddenly the pool gets deep, And little Flo calls out to ,May— The rising tide has nearly caught her, And fills her little shoes with water, ' And, see! the basket floats away! Fred, in alarm, flings down the net, And catches Flo (his darling pet), -And in his arms he holds her tight. "Grasp my jacket, May," he cries, As to gain the shore he tries And struggles on with all his might. Wet—as wet as wet can be— Stand the little shivering three, •
No prawns, no basket, and no net. Long, I think, 'twill be ere they Are allowed to go and play At catching prawns, and getting wet. ALICE InoNs.

MOVING, SOOTHING, SOOTHING, AND SATISFYING. "Yes," said the minister, "my visit v:as a great success. Between you and me, I think I satisfied them. At any rate, they never asked me again. My address was moving,_ soothing, and satisfying. 'Soon after I commenced, some people got up and walked out. That was the moving part. Most of the others went to sleep. That was the soothing part. And they never asked me again. That was the satisfying part." LIZZIE HTJGIIES.

When Meg was going on her .way to fetch her
aunt some tea, She slipped upon a piece of peel, and down, of
course, fell she. _ And then the sixpence from her hand was jerked and rolled away: It dropped between the gutter bars, to little
--Meg's dismay. - "What shall I do?' -ishe,crio aloud; then some one came along— - Her_ playmate, Harris Green—who asked her
kin* what was wrong. Aleg _told him. of her loss, and he was sorry,
this was plain: He closer went, and tried to see that sixpence
in the drain. "We cannot get it back," he sighed; "but, see,

this is for you," - • And cheerily a sixpence bright he from his pocket drew. "A gent. this morning gave it me," he said, with smiling face, "Because I held his horse while he was in the market-place." And as Meg took the shining gift, and thanked
him from her heart, They turned and saw that they were watched, and Harris gave a start. It was his gent. who stood close by, and he was pleased indeed, liecause the ladclie proved a friend to Meg in
time of need; And you can guess that Harris had a very good
reward, For all such helplul gifts as his are certainly
_ restored— On every doer of kind deeds a blessing is out- poured. G. HANCOCK.

A NOVEL TIME-PIECE.

A man who was appointed watchman at a mine in Nevada had no, watch. He did not wish to buj one, yet was desirous of knowing how the time was passing. , He borrowed the watch of a friend for one night. On returning the watch ,the next, day he told his friend that he was all right now,, that he had a timekeeper of his own. He then unrolled a strip of paper, some four .inches in width, from a stick, and exhibited it 'es his clock. On this strip of paper he had marked down, as they rose above the ,horizon. all the stars =4l constellations, within a narrow Opposite each star was the time of its making its appearance—hour and minute. The wal,chman says his watch is a fine time-keeper He has recently improved it somewhat. The slip of paper -now mils on two small rollers that are placcd in a small box, which has a eliding lid of glass. As the night wears away and the stars pass over, he now turns the crank of his watch and looke, at: the time marked by the side of each. To wind no his watch he runs the tape hack upon the initial roller.

IL AND CORRESPONDENCE.

The term "Inland Correspondence" means cor- respondence pnsted within the United Kingdom, including ths Isle of Wan and the Channel Islands. "Inland Corraspendence " is divided into the following classes : (a) Letters (d) Newspapers (b) Postcards (e) Parcels (c) Halfpenny packets Not only letters, but any document or article (with a few trifling exceptions) which can be trans- milted by post at all, may be sent by letter pott, the only limitation being that of size. LETTER POST. The prepaid rate of postage is as follows Not exceeding 4 ozs. in weight Id. Per every additional 2 0z5.... A letter posted unpaid is chargeable on delivery with double postage; a letter insufficiently paid, with double the deficiency. No letter may exceed two feet in length, one foot in width, or ono font in depth.

div.head: POST-CARDS.
div.p: POST-CARDS.

- The propaid rate of postage on every post-card is one half-penny, and on every reply post-card one penny. A post-card posted unpaid is chargeable on delivery with one penny. , Cards used as post-cards must be rusde of ordinary card-board, not thicker than the material used for the thickest official post-card. Theymay not exceed inches'in length by Si inches in width, or be less than Si inches in length by 21 inches in width. A gu nmed lsbel (not to exceed 2 iaches long and 3-inch wide) bearing the address may now be affixed to the whirl:Fig side of card. If spy of the rake relating to a post-card be infringed, the card will be treated as a letter. HALFPENNY P ACK CT POST.
The Halfpenny Packet Pest can be used only for packets not exceeding 2oz. in weight. Printed matter, &c., ngt in the nature of a letter, may be transmitted by this method. • NEWSPAPER POST. _

The prepaid rate of postage on a registered news- paper, including any supplement thereto, whether posted singly or with others is id. Newspapers not registered at the General Post Office are treated in the pcst like any other pzintecl matter.

PARCEL POST. The rates of postage on parcels areas follows: Fora parcel ... not exceeding 1 lb. 0 3 1 exceeding 1 lb. „ 2 lb. 0 4 0 lb If 3 lb. 0 5 t „ ,3 lb. The size allowed for an inland parcel is : Greatest length... ... ... 3 ft. 6 in. Greatest length and girth combined 6 ft. 0 in. For example—A parcel measuring 3ft. 6in, in its longest dimensions as much as 2ft. Gin, round its thickest part ; a short parcel may be thicker ' • thus, if it measure no more than 3ft. in length, it may measure as much as 3ft. round its thickest part. The postage on a parcel must he prepaid. Mark each parcel Parcel Post." A parcel must not be posted in a letter box, but presented at the counter of a post office, and the sender should see that the weight, size and postage are in order before leaving. PARCELS (FOREIGN AND COLONIAL). Parcels are accepted for parcel post to most foreign countries under conditions similar to the inland regulations, except that for customs require- ments the contents most be declared. The customs charges can be prepaid or collected on delivery. The postage varies to different countries and must be prepaid. Mon v ORDERS (INLAND.) The postal authorities cannot issue a single money order for more than £4O, and will only cash them at the money order &Hee at which they are made payable, unless they are crossed, when they can Le paid through a hank. No fractional part of a id. can be contnined in a money order. The :rites of poundage are :—Not exceeding £l, 2d.: £3, 3d.; £lO, 41.•, £2O, 63. ; 81. ; £4O, 101 By paying an additional 21. and cost of the telegram of advice, a money order can be telegraphed under certain restrictions. MONET ORDERS (FOREIGN AND COLONIAL.) The maximum amount for which a money order rnny be issued for places abroad varies in each particular place. The poundage rates are :—Not exceedine £l,3d. •, £2, Gd. ; and above that, 3d. for each additional £2 or portion of it. A fee of Gcl. in addition to the ordinary poundage, together with cost of telegram of advice, enables money orders to be telegraphed to certain planes abroad. POSTAL ORDERS. . .

These are obtainable at any money order eine in the United Kingdom, and possess the advantage over money orders that they can be cashed at any money order office. If crossed, they can be paid into a bank. They are issued for fixed amounts, rising by Gd., from Gd. to 21 Is. The poundage fees are : up to 2s. Gd.; Id. up to Ms.; Id. up to 21s. Before parting with a postal order, always fill in the name of the person to whom the amount is to be paid. Each order is numbered, as is also the counterfoil attached, which latter should be retained and name of payee filled in. The Post- mnater-General will entertain no further claim after an order is once paid. Stamps to the amount of sd.'can be affixed to make up Odd sums.

_ TELEGRANIS (TNLAND). The Postmaster-General possesses,almost entirely, the privilege of transrnitting,collecting and deliver- ing telegrams in the United Kingdom. 'Fhe charge for a telegram is a minimum amount of ad. which covers 12 words, and an additional id. for each extra word. This charge includes delivery within the postal district if sent out for delivery from a head telegraph office, but if from a sub-ofilce then within three miles only, beyond which a charge of 3d. per mile is made from the office door. All charges are, as far as possible, prepared by affixing stamps to telegram form.‘ Address of person receiv- ing a telegram has to be paid for, but sender'q name if written on hack of form need not he. Five figures count as one word. The cost of a reply may be prepaid. Telegrams can be repeated on payment of half the original charge, which extra payment is refunded if error is detected. Telegrams may be posted in {call or pillar boxes, or handed to rural postmen, and are wired as soon as received at the nearest telegraph office. Late fees secure attention, in certain cases, to telegrams handed in after the usual hours. The cost of registering an abbrevi- ated address, which must consist of two words, is £1 is.

TELEOR iMS (FOREIGN AND COLONIAL) Must be written on special forms and are accepted in the language of any of the principal European countries. 'Me rates vary, and are too numerous to detail here. POST OFFICE SAVINGS RANK.

These nre established at all money order offices. In ordinary cases the annual deposit must not exceed .650, end the total amount £2OO. No person can have more than one account. Amounts placed in the bank on behalf of children under seven years of age cannot be withdrawn until the child, reaches that age, and then only under his or her own signa- ture. The smallest amount received at a time is Is., and this may take the form of 12 penny stamps affixed to a special form. Each depositor receives a bank book in which the smonnt of each deposit should he entered at the time of paying in. If the deposit is £1 or over, a spacial acknowledgment is sent from the head London office. Interest is allowed at the rate of 2.1. per cent. Any amount up to and including .£1 may he withdrawn without previons notice, on presenting a bank book. The bank book should be sent each year, postage.free, on the anniversary of the date when the account was opened, to the Controller of the Savings Bank Department for purposes of checking and adding interest. The withdrawal of money can be expedited by telegraphing, the depositor paying cost of telegrams. P.O. TELEPHONE AND TRUNK LINK CHARGP,Fi. The fees for the use of the Trunk lines am as follows:— For 25 miles or under f I 50 ...............d. 7.5 f t f ff „ .. 100 ~every additional 40 raile ... —. s or fraction ~ ~ thereof... , _ _ 6d.
Between the hours of 7 p.m. and 7 a.m., six minutes convers9tlon is allowed for the same price as three minutes between '7 a.M. and 7 p.m., and a reduced charge is made for three minute calls.

MOTOR CAR AND CYCLE REqI7LATIONS. Each one must be registered with the council of a county or county borough, the fee being £1 for a motor car, and ss. for a motor cycle. A registered number is assigned to each, which it is an offence not to keep arlixed when driving. Esch driver must possess A license, casting 55., to be renewed every 12 months, and obtainable from the clunty authorities, which may be endorsed or suspended for reckless driving or certain other offences. The highest speed at which a car may be driven on the public highways is 20 miles an hour, which is reduced to 10 miles under special local regula- tions. It is an offence under, the Motor Car Act (1903), to drive a car in such a way on a public highway as to be dargerous to the public, having regard to v.II the circumstances of the case. In the event of an accident to any person due to tbn presence of the motor car on the road, the driver must supply his name and address, and the owner and number of the car, under heavy penal- ties. The driver must produce his licence at the request of a police constable.

div.p: LETTERS TO THE EDITOR.
NOTICE TO CORRESPONDENTS. Authors of letters intended for publication must in all cases send their names and addresses to the Editor as a guarantee of good faith.

div.head: Atheism at Bridge Foot.
div.p: Atheism at Bridge Foot.

Sir,—One o tbe questions at the meeting referred to by our friend J.W.B. was " What is a Christian ? " Imagine a Christian in the year of Our Lord 1908 in a Christian country after nearly 2000 years of Christian teaching asking an atheist" What is a Christian? " Is it any wonder the lecturer had no difficulty in answering? J.W.B. seems to think that Christian ministers will defend their Faith against this attack on Christianity, for he writes : " I think our local preachers should attack it. I trust if the blasphemy occurs again some reverend gentleman will settle his hash." Not being a prophet, I cannot foretell, but I think that the preachers who attack it, and the rev. gents who settle the hash of the atheistical lecturer will be conspicuous by their absence. Time will tell and I shall be pleased if lam mistaken. F. A.

Walking Day Festival. Sir,—As one who has taken a part in our local Walking Day Festival for half a century, allow me to re-echo your praise on behalf of our Chief Constable, Mr. M. Nicholls,and his officers for the splecdid order kept and arrangements carried out for the comfort of all who took part in the procession irrespective of creed. I congratulate the Church, the Roman Catholics, and the 3lissiots, Buckley-street Free Church, Ragged School and Salvation Army for the splendid manner in which they all turned out and paraded the town with the children committed to their care, numbering about nine thousand. Our Nonconformist scholars, numbering about twelve thousand, according to returns, were nil in the procession. Why this should be I laave with them, but really hope it may lead to a united rally of all sects for the future.—Yours INTERESTED.

div.head: SERVING A DRUNKEN MAN. -- Criticism of the Magistrates' Verdict
div.p: SERVING A DRUNKEN MAN. -- Criticism of the Magistrates' Verdict
At a meeting of the Executive of the Warrington Citizens' Temperance League on Wednesday evening, the appended resolution was passed, and copies ordered to he sent to the local magistrates :

div.head: RESOLUTION.
div.p: RESOLUTION.

"That in view of the lenient verdict passed by the magistrates on Monday, June 23th, in the prosecution for serving a drunken man, the Executive of the Citizens' Temperance League begs respectfully to impress upon the Borough Bench the necessity of giving the utmost support to the police in any effort they may make to reduce excessive drinking in Warrington, and to prevent offences against the Licensing Laws."

div.head: NEXT WEEK'S WIRRAL SHOW.
div.p: NEXT WEEK'S WIRRAL SHOW.

All the indications are favourable to a record success of the annual show of the Wirral and Birkenhead Agricultural Society, to be held at the Society's spacious and beautifully-situated enclosure at Bebinn,- ton on Wednesday and Thursday next, July 15th and 16th. The show promises to be of an exceptionally attractive description, for not only will the classes be more numerous and more varied than over, but the exhibits wilt includo many of the most celebrated prize winners in the country. An unique feature of this year's exhibition is that,for the first time in the history of the Society, his Majesty the King will figure among the exhibitors. The monarch will be represented by a number of prize animals from his famous herds at Windsor and Sandringham, and among them will be prize winners at the recent Royal Society's Show at Newcastle. A grand entry of dogs has been secured, and this, probably the most generally popular section of the Show, will doubtless he thronged with lovers of the friend of man " on both days. The leading exhibitors will also contest in the poultry, pigeons, rabbits, and cavies' sections, in which the , entries this year have been larger than ever. An I attractive prof.ramrae of driving and leaping competi- tions has again been prepared, and animals of the very highest class will be seen. Each afternoon there will be a parade in the arena of the prize-winning horses and cattle. On this occasion the Council of the Society have decided to make a departure from the rule which has guided them in the past, and to provide a "side attraction "in the shape of a grand Naval and Military Tournament. This will take place in the arena on each day after the horse leaping, and will, we have no doubt, afford both entertainment and instruc- tion to large crowds. All further information, in regard to prices of admission, etc., may be obtained on reference to our advertisement columns, or upon application to Mr. Arthur 11. Edwardson, Secretary, 6, Hamilton-square, Birkenhead.

div.head: Wesleyan Ministerial Changes.
div.p: Wesleyan Ministerial Changes.

The Stationing Committee of the I.Vesloyan Conference was in session at the Centenary Hall, London, on Wednesday and Thursday of last week, and the Confer- ence Committee at York issued the draft on Saturday, when copies were posted to ministers and circuit stewards all over the country. This draft is awaited with eager interest by the Wesleyan community, especially by the "700 " and more ministers who are changing circuits this year. div.head: LOCAL WEDDINGS.
div.p: LOCAL WEDDINGS.
Bleckly—Litton.

There was a very pretty wedding at All Saints Church, Daresbury, on Tuesday afternoon, when Mr. Arthur Sanderson Bleckly, eldest son of Mt. W. H. meekly, of Thelwall, was married to Miss Elizabeth Litton, of The Uplands, Moore, daughter of the late Major Litton, of Latchford. Great interest was taken in the event, the bride and bridegroom being well known and respected in the district, and a large and 1 fashionable congregation assembled. The chancel of the church had been beautifully decorated with choice flowers by Mrs. and Miss Ridgway, and Mrs. and Miss T. T. Lee-Jones. The service, which was choral, was conducted by the vicar, Rev. T. T. Lee-Jones. As a processional hymn the choir sang " Father of all, to Thee," and they afterwards rendered the tlith Psalm, "God be merciful unto us and bless us" and the hymn " May the grace of Christ our Saviour." The bride was given away by her brother Mr. T. U. Litton, and as her maids she had Miss Frances Litton (sister) and Miss Ethel Bleckly (cousin of the bride- groom). Mr. Percy Meekly (brother) discharged the duties of best man and Mr. Frank Williamson, of Thelwall, acted as groomsman. A pleasing selection of organ music, including the Bridal March from " Lohengrin" and Mendelssohn's Wedding March,was played by Dr. Reginald Smith (brother-in-law of the bride). As the wedding party left for the Uplands, where a reception was held, the church bells rang a merry peal. During the afternoon the bride and bridegroom departed for Scotland. Many handsome presents were received including a massive silver salver frcm the managers, foremen and chief work- men of the Iron and Steel Department of the Pearson and Knowles Coal and Iron Co., Ltd.

div.head: Bat€—Bolton.
div.p: Bat€—Bolton.

The marriage was solemnized at the Warrington Parish Church, on Monday, of Mr. William lAewellyn Bate, son of Mr. Frederick Bate, 121, Marshhouse-lane and Miss Margaret Gou'den Bolton, adopted daughter of Mr. Robert Bolton, 83, Manchester-road. A large congregation witness: d the ceremony. The Rector (Rev. Canon Willis) officiated. The bride, who was given away by Mr. Robert Bolton, was charmingly attired in cream silk,trinamed with costly embroidered chiffon and silk insertion,and carried a lovely bouquet of lilies and orchids. She was attended by two brides- maids—Misses Gertrude and Lily Smith—whose dresses were of cream striped voile trimmed with Valenciennes lace. Their bouquets were composed of roses. Mr. William Stitch discharged the duties of best man. Mr. F. M. Darby, Mus. Bac., was at the organ and at the close of the service he played Mendelssohn's Wedding March. As the happy couple ' left the church the bells rang a merry peal. The wedding party was photographed by Mr. James Parkinson in the Rectory grounds, kindly placed at their disposal by the Rector. All the guests wore button-holes of very choice orchids, the gifts of Alderman Bolton. The reception was held at Atkinson's Cs f, Bridge-street, about fifty guests attending. The catering gave complete satisfaction. The usual toasts were enthusiastically honoured and the festivities continued until 11 pm. The happy couple left for Blackpool, at 6.30 p.m., the bride's travelling dress being of green crepe-do-chene. Many handsome presents were received, including a cheque from Mr. Robert Bolton. The bridegroom's present to the bride was a gold bangle set with diamonds, and the bride's present to the bridegroom was a valuable g3ld albert. The bridegroom's gifts to the bridesmaids were gold brooches.

Atkinson—Scotson. There was a pretty wedding at Holy Trinity Church on Thursday, when Mr. Mowbray Atkinson, of Coventry, was married to Miss Eleanor Mary Scotson, daughter of Mr. James Seotson, Bold-street, Warring- ton. The ceremony was witnessed by a large congre- gation, the Vicar (Rev. E. C. E. Carleton) officiating. The bride, who was given away by her father, was charmingly attired in a cream cloth dress, trimmed with white and gold, with white picture hat, and , carried a lovely bouquet of white roses, heliotrope and orange blossom. She was attended by three bridesmaids —Miss Amy Garnett, of Stockton Heath, and the Misses Winifred Scotson (niece of the bride) and Phyllis Lightburn. Miss Garnett was attired in a white needlework robe, with black hat,and her bouquet was composed of sweet peas. She wore a handsome gold bangle, the gift of the bridegroom. The two juvenile bridesmaids wore pretty white embroidered dresses, over pale blue silk, and bonnets trimmed with pink roses and forget-me-nots. They carried bouquets of carnations and their ornaments were gold brooches, the flirts of the bridegroom. Mr. Robertson, of Frodshatn and Warrington, discharged the duties of best man. Mr. Randall was at the organ and played the Wedding March as the bridal party left the church. The wedding breakfast was served in Holy Trinity Church Institute. Later the happy couple left for London, where the honeymoon is being spent, tho bride's going-away dress being a mauve costume with hat to match.

Shakeshaft—Mullard. The Parish Church of St. Mary at Lymm was the scene of a fashionable wedding on Wednesday, when Mr. Denis Shakeshaft, son of Mr. Joseph Shakeshaft, of Lymtn, was married to Miss llilda Maria Mallard, daughter of Mr. W. Mallard, clerk to the Lymm Urban District Council. The large congrega- tion was a testimony to the popularity of the bride and bridegroom. The Rector (Rev. G. B. Thurston) officiated. The bride, who was given away by her father, was beautifully gowned in white silk, trimmed with broderie Anglais and lace insertion. She wore a veil and wreath of orange blossom and carried a handsome shower bouquet of white roses and lilies, the gift of the bridgroom. Her ornaments were a gold bracelet, given by the bride- groom, and a diamond pendant, a present from her father. She was attended by three bridesmaids Miss Maud Mullard (sister of the bride), Miss Mabel Miller, of Bedford (cousin of the bride), and the charming little daughter of Dr. de Jong, of Lymm. Their dresses were of heliotrope voile, with silk and velvet trimmings, with chiffon and gold embroidery, and they carried shower bouquets of sweet peas. Their ornaments were gold safety pin brooches, the gifts of the bridegroom. Mr. Harry Saville, of Lymm, acted as best man. Mr. Cook presided at the organ, and played choice selections, including Mendelssohn's Wedding March. After the ceremmy, a reception was held at the Masonic Hall, upwards of sixty guests attending. Later the happy couple left for North Wales,where the honeymoon is being spent. The bride's travelling dress was of cream serge, with picture hat. div.head: Examiner, Saturday, July 11, 1908.
div.p: The Examiner, Saturday, July 11, 1908.
PEN KETH.

SUNDAY Smoot, TEACHERS' Trtir.—The teachers and officers of the Wesleyan Sunday school went for their annual trip on Saturday, the place chosen being Windermere. The party which numbered 30 left Penketh at 4.30 a.m. by 'bus to Bank Quay,leaving there at 5.30 a.m. They arrived at Windermere at 3 o'clock and they walked to Bowness where they had breakfa.A. Proceeding by steamer to Ambleside they stayed about an hour, then by steamer to Lakeside. They then left for Newby Bridge, some of the young excursionists in rowing boats, whilst others preferred to walk in order 'to obtain a better view of the beautiful scenery. On arriving at the Swan Hotel tea was served at 3.30. The return journey was commenced at about 5.40 p.m. Penketh being reached at eleven o'clock. The arrange- ments had been in the hands of Mr. Mark Ray, to whom great praise is due, for all were agreed that a most enjoyable day had been spent. SANKEY CIIORAL CLASS.—The members of the Sankey Choral Class held their annual trip on Saturday. Between 40 and 50 members and a few friends left Sankey Station at 9.30 a.m. by special train for South- port. In the forenoon the various places of interest were visited, and at 12 noon the party assembled at Rountree's Cafe, Lord-street, for dinner. This over, the members separated, some going to the beach, and others to the Churchtovvn gardens. Tea was served at five o'clock, and the party left about nine. The weather was ideal, and all reached home safely and in good time. PRESENTATION TO MISS DA UNT.—The members of the Women's Guild have made a wedding gift to Miss Daunt, The Elms, Penketh. After singing "Lead us, Heavenly Father, lead us," the Rev. J. R. Jones (president) briefly opened the proceedings. Mrs. Owen, on behalf of the members, wished Miss Daunt much happiness and every good wish, and handed to her a handsome set of oak trays, a brass plant stand,plant and an illuminated card (the work of Mr. R. Routledge), hearing the inscription: "Presented to Miss Alice do Tracy Daunt, by the members of St. Mary's Women's Guild, Penketh, on the occasion of her marriage, July, 1308." Miss Daunt and Miss Tinsley thanked the members for their handsome gifts. WALKING DAY.—Friday last was a day of great enjoyment for the children. Walking day is eagerly looked forward to and one could see that all the villagers, with their gaily decorated houses, intended to do their part to make the day a success. For several years the festival has been somewhat marred by the inclement weather, the glorious sunshine of Friday 1 being an agreeable change. The procession a hich was divided into two sections, viz., Sankey St. Mary's and Penketh Mission, and Penketh Wesleyan Sunday school was quite in keeping with past years. The procession of the Church and Mission commenced aboat 1 o'clock from the Mission. The Wesleyans started about 2 o'clock both being headed by a band. The Wesleyans made their usual halt at Mr. Parker's and were provided with a drink of lemonade which was much enjoyed. About half an hour was well spent admiring the flowers, the roses being a perfect show. The procession then pro- ceeded to the schools for tea. The Church children after tea went to the Vicarage, Great Sankey, and the Wesleyan children to the Penketh Recreation grounds, where games and sports were indulged in. The sports results were as follows :-50 yards handicap race for boys 7to 9 : 1, H. Pearson ; 2, S. Richardson ;3, R. Loxley. For girls : 1, E. Long; 2, Ruth Loxley ; 3, A. Almond. 70 yards race for boys 10 to 12 : 1, J. Long ; 2, J. Irwin ; 3, G. Carrington. Girls : 1, W. Foden; 2, A. Foden ; 3, B. Walters. 80 yards (13 to 17) : 1, H. Phimpton ; 2, A. Mellor ; 3, H. Wood. Girls : 1, G. Bell ; 2, W. Watson ; 3, B. Watson. 100 yards (17 and over) : 1, F. Davies ; 2, W. Tucker ; 3, EL Shaw. The sack race was won by :-1, S. Shaw ; 2, H. Wood ; 3, J. Walker. Jumping (from 9 to 11), J. Long ; 12 to 14, H. Wood ; 15 to 17, H. Plumpton ; 17 and over, W. Tucker and H. Molyneux, divided. Young ladies race, 17 and over was won by Miss Parker, 1 ; Miss E. Wood, 2 ; Miss M. Dodds, 3. The prizes, which were given on the field to the little children, were provided by Mrs. Dodds. The races over, all made their way to the Wesleyan Schools, where the other winners were presented with their prizes by Mrs. Withinshaw, the prizes being provided by the members of the Men's Bible Class, who undertake the work of the sports ; those responsible this year being Messrs. Foden, Long, Bell, Aldcroft, Hughes, Wood, Ireland, Walters and Clay. After all had received their prizes each one was given a bag containing nuts, sweets, and biscuits. This brought a most enjoyable day to a close.

div.head: ROYAL COURT THEATRE.
div.p: ROYAL COURT THEATRE.
Third Week of Mr. Ryder Boys' Season

Mr. Ryder Boys' company have given further evidence of their versatility this seek by presenting another most interesting series of plays. On Monday and Tuesday evening " The Lady of Lyons " was staged with great success. Lord Lytton's drama loans none of its hold on the theatre-going public and its many powerful scenes held the audiences spell- bound. Mr. Henry Worrall, who has establised him- self in the favour a all who have seen Mr. Boys' productions here, was an admirable Claude Melnotte, while Miss Alice Hughes added to her laurels by a fine portrayal of Pauline. On Wednesday evening there was a complete change, in the shape of Sydney Grundy's play "A Fool's Paradise." It is the story of a man who, thinking that he possesses a perfect treasure of a wife, is all the while being slowly poisoned by her in order that she may acquire his wealth and marry another. Her infamy is discovered just in time to save the husband, and she is so mortified at the failure of her scheme that she takes her own life. The outstanding char- acter in the play is Sir Peter Lund, the physician, and this was in the hands of Mr. Harold Neville, an actor of undoubted talent. It was a pity that his clever study was somewhat marred by little lapses of memory. Miss Ethel Norhury took the part of Beatrice Selwyn most capably, while Miss Elsie Vrou's natural and vivacious portrayal of Kate Derwent captivated the audience. Mr. Alan Mudie as Lord Normantower, Mr. Murray Graham as Hon. Tom Verinder, and Miss Betty Noel as Mildred Selwyn all realized the humour of their respective parts. Mr Leonard Mudie was well placed as Philip Selwyn. The balcony scene from " Romeo and Juliet" was given as a curtain raiser, Mr. Henry Worrell and Miss Elsie Vron acquitting themselves with credit. On Thurs- day evening there was a special attraction, Gold- smith's comedy " She stoops to conquer" being presented. Mr. Ryder Boys as Old Hardcastle had a role which eminently suited him, and he enhanced his reputation. The other characters were in capable hands. Last evening "A Fool's paradise " was repeated. To-night (Saturday) "The Lady of Lyons" will again be played, and those who desire a dramatic treat should make a point of witnessing the perform- ance.

div.head: NEXT WEEK'S PROGRAMME.
div.p: NEXT WEEK'S PROGRAMME.

Mr. Ryder Boys' Company enter upon their fourth and last week here next Monday and the programme announced is about the most attractive they have yet submitted. On Monday evening the ever popular " David Garrick "will be presented and the powerful cast will include Mr. Leonard Mudie as Garrick, Mr. Ryder Boys as Gresham, Mr. Henry Worrall as Tallyhant, and Miss Elsie Vron as Violet. On Wednesday and Thursday evenings the attraction will be Pinero's celebrated play " The Money Spinner," Mr. Harold Neville appearing as Baron Croodle (as played by Sir John Hare), and Miss Elsie Vron as Millicent: On Friday and Saturday "Jane," said to be the funniest farce ever written, will be presented ; with Miss Betty Noel as Jane and Mr, Alan Mudie as Charlie Shackleton. " Jane " is one scream from start to finish. It has been Harry Nichols' greatest success. He has played it at the Comedy Theatre, where it had an enormous run. , After next Saturday the theatre will be closed for a fortnight for renovation; and will re-open on August Bank Holiday with a special London production.

div.head: SEQUEL TO A MOTOR ACCIDENT.
div.p: SEQUEL TO A MOTOR ACCIDENT.
County Court Action at Warrington.

At the Warrington County Court on Thursday, before his Honour Judge Shiress Will,K.C.,and a jury,Ada Smith, widow, 9, West View, Orford, sued Charles Eckersley, Fulwood, Great Orme-road, Llandudno, for damages for personal injuries sustained by being knocked down by a motor car.—Mr. F. Cuthbert Smith, barrister (instructed by Mr. T. S. Steel) appeared for the ,1 plaintiff, and Mr. J. H. Graham, barrister (instructed by Mr. Oswald S. Hickson, London) represented the defendant.

Mr. Cuthbert Smith said that in consequence of the accident plaintiff was incapable of following the employment on which she depended for a livelihood. She had previously earned her living by upholstering and sewing. On December 31st last she was going along Winwick-road in the direction of Winwick. She started to cross the road from the corner of Jockey- street in order to reach Kerfoot-street. The road was a good wide road and gave plenty of room for traffic and pedestrians. When she started to cross the road, a horse and cart were coming out of Jockey-street on their proper side of the road towards Warrington. She took a diagonal line in order to avoid the 1 vehicle and she was about a yard Irons the kerb on the Kerfoot-street side when the defendant's motor car, which was driven by his man, came along behind her, without blowing the horn or giving any warning of its approach, on the wrong side of the road, and knocked her down, dragging her some two or three yards. In fairness to the defendant it must be stated that the car was pulled up quickly. The plaintiff was taken home in the car. The injuries brought on internal bleeding, and her left hand had become so numb that she could not use it properly, and was incapable of earning a penny piece. There was no reason in the world why defendant should have driven on the wrong side. Although there was no absolute right or wrong side of the road in law, still if a man were found driving on his wrong side without any reasonable excuse it raised a prima facie case of negligence against him. Defendant's 1 chauffeur was driving at ton great a speed considering the spot at which the accident took place. On January Ist defendant wrote to plaintiff's son enclosing a t cheque for three guineas and stating that he felt sorry Ifor the plaintiff. He added : "At the same time your mother is quite at liberty to make any claim for the injury she has sustained so far as lam concerned. If your mother should obtain anything, the insurance company wonld pay it. I am quite certain my driver was not at all to blame." Further cor- respondence ensued and in one letter defendant reiterated that his driver was not to blame. He added "It was a mercy she was not killed. I am insured against accident but I feel sure your mother would not be able to substantiate any claim." Later the mattter was placed in the hands of the insurance company whose representative (Mr. Bursey) wrote stating that there was no liability whatever on the part of Mr. Eckersley and the accident was due entirely to the negligence of Mrs, Smith. He added "This was admitted by her own son in writing and I have that letter before me." Mr. Smith asked for the letter to be produced. Mr. Graham said the letter did not appear to exist. The insuranc3 company's representative must have got mixed up with another claim. Mr. Smith added that in the letter Mr. Bursey characterised Mrs. Smith's claim as" the usual sort of begging letter which inevitably follows an occurrence of this kind."

Plaintiff, who is 59 years of age, was then called and gave evidence bearing out counsel's statement. Robert Fleming Clarke, of Aughton, near Ormskirk, book keeper in the manager's office of the Cheshire Lines Committee, said he was collecting rents in Winwick-road on December 31st and saw defendant's car approaching at what he considered to be a dangerous speed. It was much above the average speed of a tram car. The motor car was two-thirds of the way from the left-hand side of the road when he first saw it, and when it struck the plaintiff it was a yard from the kerb on the right hand side. He did not hear the horn sounded. At that spot the road widened, so that there was ample room for the car to pass. Witness said to the driver : "This is your fault. You were going too quickly," and he replied "I was not going above my regulation speed." George IL Sheldon, milk dealer, said the car was "fair bouncing" when it passed him, about 300 yards before reaching the scene of the accident. Alfred Dunbobbin, shoe maker, said the car was going over 20 miles an hour at a quarter of a mile from where the accident occured. Witness took the number of the car as he expected it to knock someone down before it reached the Horse and Jockey." Questioning the witness as to the speed, Mr. Graham asked "I suppose you have heard of cyclists being brought up and fined for scorching?" Witness: Not since motor cars came in. (Laughter.) Dr. Ferguson described the plaintiff's injuries. He said she was a strong healthy woman before the accident. When he examined her, the left arm, shoulder and side were very tender and she suffered a great deal of pain from them. The lower part of the body was severely injured and there was internal bleeding. Plaintiff was in bed three weeks.

\William Smith,i;l;int-ifFs.;;;;.was also called. For the defence George Stewart Whiteford, driver of the car, stated that he had been driving for twelve years—ever since motor cars were first Introduced in Scotland. When approaching Warrington on the date of the accident he was travelling at not more than 12 miles an hour. He sounded his born several times between Longford Bridge and the "Horse and Jockey." He was driving on the tram lines. In order to avoid the horse and cart coming out of Jockey-street he was obliged to swing across to the right side of the road. He saw plaintiff come from behind the cart and sounded his born and slowed down to seven or eight miles an hour. Plaintiff jumped forward and walked into the car. When she was picked up he asked her if she was hurt, and she said : " Oh, no, I ant not hurt at all. It was not your fault. It was entirely my own." Charles Eckersley, the defendant, was then called and said he had a great objection to driving at high speeds and his chauffeur always had instructions to enter towns slowly. Whiteford was a very careful driver and sounded the born so often that it was a perfect nuisance. They bad never had an accident of that kind with the car before. Witness bore out Whiteford's account of the accident and said that when asked if she was hurt witness said " Oh, no. Only a little shaken." Joseph Pullocic, the driver of the horse and cart, said Mrs. Smith did not appear to see the car and stepped in front of it. George Syers, road sweeper, said he hoard the horn sounded and he moved in consequence. Ambrose Wilkinson said the driver did all in his power to draw the car up at once, in fact witness never saw a cleverer thing in his life." Mr. Graham, in addressing the jury, asked them to set aside any prejudices they might have against motor cars.

His Honour having summed up, the jury returned a verdict for the plaintiff with £5O damages (to include £l2 17s. which the defendant admitted in the event of judgment being given against him) and costs. The foreman(Mr.James Critcbley) said the jury desired to know if the chauffeur had ever been in trouble before as, if not, they did not wish his licence to be endorsed. His Honour said that was not a Police Court and it was not within his power to endorse a licence.

div.head: PRINCESS TRIXTE ASTONISTIES VIE KING AND QUEEN.
div.p: PRINCESS TRIXTE ASTONISTIES VIE KING AND QUEEN.

Conscious apparently of the fact that she had proved herself a thinking horse to the absolute satisfaction of his Majesty the King and incidentally described tho colour of the handsome gown worn by her Majesty Queen Alexandra, Princess Trish) the most remarkable horse in all the world returned to the White City on Tuesday afternoon from Buckingham Palace, where she was commanded to perform on Monday afternoon by his Majesty in honour of Princess Victoria's birthday party to a score of her royal playmates. No other horse in all the world received such an ovation as did Princess Trixie during her special performance before the Royal Family on Monday. As a special mark of attention Trixie was placed at the head of the after- noon's programme arranged by the King in person. The entertainment was given on the beautiful green sward at Buckingham Palace and more than 100 children of royal parentage were grouped about the improvised ring. Mr. Barnes and Trixie were given a cordial greeting when they made their appearance direct from the 'White City in Manchester. The children applauded v;gourously when Trixie summoned school by ringing a big bell, and went into hysterics of joy as she spelled out the names of many of England's future royal heads. The climax came however when Mr. Barnes asked the animal to describe the color of the gown worn by Queen Alexandra, who with the King stood some distance away. Trixie gazed intently at her Majesty for a few seconds then lower- ing her head picked from an assortment of colours a lavender ribbon. The wonderful horse had truly matched the gown worn by the Queen, and no one applauded more vigourously than did the King and Queen. Trixie further distinguished herself by telling the correct time of day after looking at a watch held by a member of the Royal Family. The thinking horse and her smiling owner were given much hearty applause as they bowed out of the arena and prepared to start back to Man- chester's White City. 'I feel that I have at last been well rewarded for the 18 long years I spent in develop- ing Trixie's intelligence "said Mr. Barnes on his return. "Never shall I forget the gracious reception given me and my pet by the much beloved King and Queen of England. As an American citizen my reception touched me deeply and I am almost convinced that frixie too laboured under the influence of having ben signally honoured for she worked most beautifully throughout the performance."

div.head: WORKS ASSESSMENTS.
div.p: WORKS ASSESSMENTS.
More Heavy Increases at Warrington.

A meeting of the Warrington Union Assessment Committee was held at the Workhouse yesterday morn- ing, Mr. J. Billings presiding. There were also present :—Messrs. G. Mather, W. Houghton, W. Gill, A. Brooks, NV. Furness, R. Forshaw, A. Bottomley (clerk to the Guardians), R. R. Meacock (valuer), W. H. Woodcock (assistant overseer.)

APPOINTMENT OF CLERK. Mr. A. BROOKS moved the appointment of Mr. Bottomley as clerk to the committee. He said those who had come into contact with him had formed a very favourable opinion of his abilities, and of his intention to do his best for the Union. Mr. W. HOUGHTON seconded._ _ _ .
Mr. MATER said he was fully persuaded that Mr. Bottomley was a worker, and would discharge the duties to their satisfaction. .
The resolution was agreed to. It was decided to adjourn the question of remunera- tion pending the receipt of information as to the amounts paid by other authorities.

WARRINGTON WIRE ROPE CD, LTD. Mr. H. H. FULLER, of London, appealed on behalf of the Warrington Wire Rope Co., Ltd., against their assessment of £lll gross and £361 ratable. The old valuation was £320 10s. gross and £258 103. ratable. The CHAIRMAN asked why the Company objected to this slight increase ? Mr. FULLER: What you might think slight we might think very heavy. Continuing, he said the Company thought it was an unnecessary increase altogether, because the works were old works. They were almost entirely composed of a few old brick buildings and some light sheds, some of which were corrugated iron and had been erected quite recently. What the firm held was the value of the works at the present time was £lOO gross and they took from that 50 per cent, leaving a ratable value of £2OO per annum. The land was lease- hold, the area being 4,500 yards and the rent £37 4s. 2d. There was one access from the railway, the length of the siding being 127 yards. In arrriving at their figures the Committee only allowed £BO per annum for main- tenance and repairs, but he submitted it should be £2OO. It was decided to adjourn the appeal in order that the valuer might confer with Mr. Fuller. _ _

LONG collo WIRE CO., LTD, Mr. FULLER then appealed against the assessment of the Longford Wire Company, Limited, at £2,110 gross and 21,631 ratable. The previous valuation was £1,071 gross and £BlO ratable. The CHAIRMAN : A slight increase there, Mr. Fuller. Mr. FULLER : Everything seems to be slight with you. (Laughter). Whether it is slight or heavy, the fact remains that it has been doubled and my clients instruct me that they are very much astonished, first of all that one class of works should be valued and not the whole place. The CHAIRMAN : It is not possible for one valuer to value all the works in the Union at the same time. Mr. FULLER : It is possible for you to arrange for a valuation to be made of the whole Union and to pat all the valuations in force together, so that one class of works has not to bear a larger proportion of the burdens of industry. Continuing he said the firm contended that the present was an inoppor- tune time for the re-valuation, as trade was bad and the works were running about half-time. It was true they had been remodelling and reorganiz- ing the works, but they were doing such a small amount of work that they were not using any of the extra power. The assessment had been increased from time to time as extensions had been made and it seemed

extraordinary that it should he doubled now. He was informed that an endeavour was being made to bring new trades into the town and to go and increase assessments by cent, per cent, seemed to his clients,and he thought to any reasonable person, to be pulling the extreme ends of the wire rope. (Laughter.) The firm were much dissatisfied with the assessment and they could not possibly let it stand at anything like that figure. The view they took was that the gross assess- ment should be not exceeding £l5OO and the ratable , value £750. Mr. WOODCOCri: Then you agree it is something like £5OO under-assessed on the gross and that there was a necessity for re-valuation. Mr. FULLER: I don't suggest for a moment that there is not a reasonable ground for re-assessment but if you are re-assessing you must look at the thing all round. In answer to Mr. Maacock, Mr. FULLER said the rent of the land was £l2O a year. The Comniittee also adjourned this case for a confer- ence between the valuer and Mr. Fuller. MONKS, HALL AND CO., LTD,

Mr. AI. B. LEWIS appealed on 'behalf of Messrs. Monks, Ilan and Co., Ltd., against the assessment of their works at £1,189 gross and £2,91 ratable (for the added area, formerly outside the Borough boundary) and £4,358 gross and £3,241 ratable (for the remainder of the works). lie said the present total assess- ment was £3,336 10s., so that taking the new assessment at £6,186, the increase was £2,849 103., or over 85 per cent. No changes had taken place at the works to justify any such increase and his directors felt compelled to ask for a substantial reduction. They regretted that the Dlrticulars which had been supplied in past years as to how the new valuation had been arrived at, had not been given on

this occasion. There had been some replacements in the works but no extensions. The Ist extension was made in November last when the rateable value was increased by £392. The CHAIRMAN: You ara of opinion that the assessment is about £lOO too much ? . _

Mr. LEWIS : We say it is an increase of 85 per cent. and we don't know of anything that will justify any increase. The firm, Mr. Lewis added, employed from 1,000 to 1,200 people. _After the Committee had discussed the matter, the . _ _ . .

Chairman informed Mr. Lewis that they werO of opinion that ho had not produced any tangible evidence against the assessment as it now stood. If he thought it advisable to bring further information before them at the next meeting they would ba pleased to consider it.

div.head: TRIP DAY.
div.p: TRIP DAY.
Works Excursions from Warrington.
Saturday was Warrington's annual trip clay and large numbers of the townspeople betook themselves to various holiday roam ts, Blackpool being first favourite.

BIONICS, BALL AND CO., LTD. The e:nployees and friends of the above firm, to the number of 70), went in spacial trains to Blackpool, where a most enjoyable day was spent. Blackpool was reached at 7.30 a.m., and the excursionists safely returned to ‘Varrington at 9.3). Mr. J. Sisson acted as secretary to the Trip Committee.

ARMITA-GE AND RIGBY, LTD. The employes of Messrs. Armitage and Rigby, Ltd., to the number of 1,800, journeyed to Blaclrpsol, to i which place they were conveyed n three special trains by the Cheshire Lines Committee. Charming weather was experienced, and visits were paid to the places of amusements, the piers and sands. Mr. William lVarhurton acted as socr3tary to the Trip Committee.

RICHMOND GAS STOVE AND METER CO. After their lengthy trip to Dublin last year to visit the hish ludustries Exhibition, the employes this year voted for a shorter excursion, and Blackpool was almost unanimously selected. On arrival at Blackpool the managers, foremen, and heads of departments were entertained to breakfast by Mr. Ransome, at the Bee Restaurant, Central Beach, after which they disposed of the time as they pleased. The trip was quite as popular as those which have preceded it. Two special trains were engaged, and a large number of ticket were dis- posed of by the employes amongst their friends. ST. fIELEN3 CABLE AND RUBBER COAPANY.

The °Mee 'and works staff of the St. Helens Cable and Rubber Company, Ltd., Bank guy, and the outside staff; altogether to the number of 51, wont in saloon carriages to Blackpool, which was reached shortly after eight o'clock. During tha morning some journeyed to Lytham, and others to Fleetwood and St. Anne's-on- the-sea, and at 12 all met at the Hotel Metropolo, at Blackpool, for dinner, where a hearty vote of thanks was, on the motion of Mr. Ormand, of the office staff, and seconded by Mr. Price, of the works staff, passed to Mr. Kenyon, the sezretary and manager of the company, and Mrs. Kenyon, for their kindness and presence. During the afternoon a visit was paid to the South Shore and the various places of amusement, after which a good tea was enjoyed. A start was made for home at 8.30, and it was reached in good time, a most enjoyable ' day having been spent. Mr. Charles 'Ford acted as secretary to the Trip Committee.
WILLIAM ROBERTSON, LIMITED, LATCEIFORD

The sixth annual picnic in connection with this corn- ' pany took place on Saturday last, the rendezous thisl time being the well favoured resort of Blackpool. The I picnic, both in point of numbers and everything else, I was a decided success. There was a record muster of about 160, who left Latchford by special cars at 5.45 a.m. proceeding from Bank Quay Station at 6.15 a.m. After a good run Blackpool was reached at 7.50 a.m. and to the delight of the pleasure seekers the weather was quite suitable for the occasion. The early arrival allowed ample time for the morning enjoyment of the various sights of the town, besides materi- ally contributing to a keenness of appetite for the dinner which was served in the Victoria Hall in the Winter Gardens at 11.30 21.131. There were present at this function Mr. W. Robertson (the chairman and managing director of the Company) and Mrs. Robertson, Mr. F. W. Wareing (the manager) and Mrs. Wareing,and Mr. I'. Collins (the secretary) and Mrs. Collins. The excellent dinner which was provided by the Winter Gardens Company, was fully enjoyed. The repast being over, Mr. Wareing expressed his pleasure at being once again present at the annual picnic, and hoped that all would have a very enjoyable day. They would no doubt be pleased to have the Chairman of the Company in their midst on that day. He thought their best thanks were due to their

THE SCOTTISH EXEIIBITION.

The Scottish National Exhibition still continue along the road of success, and special attractions are frequently being arranged to cater for the visitors who are coming into the Scottish capital from all pirts of the country. The band programmes are very strong. The famous Berlin Philharmonische Bias Orchestra have just finished up a very successful fortnight and this week the band of the Royal Scots Greys and the 2.nd Life Guards have been providing the outdoor music, whilst Herr Morgann's Blue Hungarian Band has daily given selections in the Concert Hall. Special organ recitals and concerts are of alrnost daily occurrence. Bands already booked to appear include the Black Dike, Coldstream Guards, Northumberland Hussars, Ist Black Watch and Irish Guard.T. On Saturday next one of the most important of Scottish Athletic events will take place in the sports enclosure,when the fourteenth annual championship between Scotland and Ireland will be decided. The most prominent athletes of both countries- will appear.

SIR J. BRUNNER, M.P., ON RAILEFAY NATIONALISATION. In a communication to the "Gas World" in favour of the nationalisation of our railways, Sir John Brunner:- M.P., writs :—" The German State railways, as a whole, pay over C per cent., whereas British and Irish railways, as a whole, pay less than 4 per cent., fu spite of higher rates for goods. I res—at least, so it appears to me— as clearly as any man can see, the political risks of Government management of the railways. I allude to the pressure which might be brought to bear on mem- bers of Parliament to put State servants into a position of unfair advantage as compared with the servants of private employers. But this difficulty is fur from insuperable. A reference to that portion of the Canals Bill describing the composition of the canals trust indicates one way of escap- ing the evils of political pressure. The pro- visions of the bill, in this particular, were the out- come of careful consideration by the very representative committee which, during three years, devoted attention to the subject. The canals trust, so composed, would have been a very independent body. A similarly com- posed body for the management of State railways would be equally independent. There is also the risk of a general strike of the railway workers. As to this, I have to say that there are some things which men must not do, and the organisation of such a general strike is one of these. It would be constructive murder. Fortunately, however, means can be found to secure for them bir play, such as we all should desire. After long years of pondering over this matter, I am profoundly convinced that the greatest need of our trade is cheap inland transit. On the sea no have beaten the whole world; on land, almost the whole world has beaten us."

Alleged False Pretences at Croft. At the Newton-le-Willows Petty Sessions on , Thursday, William Love Jones, of no settled addresS, was charged with obtaining Li is. from peter Ingham, of South View, Croft, by false pretencee- It was stated that prisoner went to prosecutor's house , and purported to be a traveller for a certain firm of booksellers in Manchester. Prosecutor agreed to purchase some " Commentaries on the Bible," and , paid £1 is. on account. The books did not arrive when prisoner had stated they would and on going to Manchester to inquire prosecutor found that prisoner . was not employed by the firm at all. Prisoner had previously been in the employ of the firm, but wan discharged two years ago.—lnspector Innes, in asking for a remand, said that prisoner was wanted all over - the country.

worthy secretary, Mr. Collins, for the excellent arrangements made, and also to Mr. Smith, Mr. Humphreys and Mr. Caldwell for their assistance. They would no doubt be very pleased to see Mr. Humphreys back amongst them after his recent serious illness, and he hoped that he would see another 20 or 30 years in their midst. (Applause.) He also thought that the thanks of the Company were duo to the Winter Gardens, and especially to their Mr. Smith, for the excellent way in which the catering had been managed. Mr. Robertson, who was received with applause, said he desired to extend to the Company his very heartiest wishes for a very enjoyable day, and he fully supported all that Mr. Wareing had said. He was pleased to see so many present looking so well, and he hoped they would all return home to Warrington safely. He sup- ported all that Mr. Wareing had said wtth regard to the management of the picnic,and also the catering. Mr. Collins, replying on behalf of himself, air. Smith and Mr. Humphreys, thanked the party for the manner in which they had acknowledged the work done in connection with the picnic. On behalf of the workmen 'be expressed the pleasure it was to all to have Mr, Robertson and Mr. Wareing at their annual function and their presence at that table was an augury of th interest and good-will they felt in the welfare of theic employees, and he hoped that they would always have them amongst them on such occasions. There was a long afternoon for the enjoyment of the varied attractions of this popular holiday place. The return journey was commenced at 9.25 p.m. the train being about half an hour late, and Warrington was reached at about 11.30 p.m., all going home with memories of what was really a very enjoyable day. • NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS. Cricket. It is a pleasant change to be able to congratulate Warrington on a highly creditable victory. They proved altogether superior to Stanley in a League engagement on Saturday and ran up a majority of 31. Let us hope this will be the beginning of many successes. They would certainly be welcomed. The winning of the toss by Mr. Silcock proved a happy augury. The spin of the coin has generally gone against Warrington of late, with disastrous results. The Stanley wicket is not beloved of cricketers and on Saturday it was in such a state that the ball flew about deneerously and the batsmen was always at a disadvantage. Going to the wicket first, Warrington compiled 85, Cresswell being the top scorer with 20 to his credit. T. Wright was responsible for 17, J. Callon for 15 and H. Callon for 14. The home eleven made a poor show, all being dismissed for a total of 51 runs, A. H. Loggie (10) and R. Lightfoot (11) being the only batsmen to get double figures. The Rev. H. Gray was the most succecsful bowler' capturing seven of the Stanley wickets for 23 rune. For Stanley Howarth got four wickets for 27 runs, and S. G. Moore six wickets for 53 runs. -- St. Helens Rees head the League, and they have only won four matches out of nine. Warrington ought to be occupying a much higher position than the fifth, hut they have been in very indifferent form se far, their record reading :—Played 7, won 2, lost 3, drawn 2, points G. The all-conquering Warrington 2nd added another to their list of victories on Saturday, Stanley 2nd being vanquished in summary fashion. The feature of the game was the excellent batting on a fi.iry wicket by Messrs. B. Pierpeint, S. Baxter, \V. V. Tarton, and T. Houghton. Baxter and Turton added 57 runs for the fifth wicket, and at 108 both fell, the former hitting five fours in his 38. Against Warrington's aggregate of 121 the Stanley men could only respond with 43, no member getting into double figures. J. Waywell anl W. Bennett bowled unchanged, and the former came out with the splendid figures of seven wickets for 20 runs, Bennett capturing the remainder at a cost of 20 runs. The fielding of the home side was exceptionally smart, and special mention should be made of the catches made by Ilawtin and Dolan. -- St. James's retain their proud position at the top of the Warrington and District League, having won five and drawn one match out of six, with 11 points to their credit. Cheshire Lines Enginees come next with 9 points. On Saturday the Engineers encountered Walker's Brewery and proved victorious by 22. 11. Brown (17), E. Dooley (14) and J. Duckworth (11) were the most successful batsmen for the winners, whilst E. Allen and Griffin each made 13 for the Brewery. The " Guardian " eleven had no difficulty in dispos- ing of Wilderspool Brewery who were beaten to the extent of 62 runs. C. Woodhead (31), Burrell (25 not out) and Ditchfield (10) batted finely, and C. Woodhead and Burrell bowled well, taking five wickets for 18 runs and four wickets for five runs respectively. -- There were lower friendly matches than usual, the fact that so many people were holiday-making no doubt rendering it difficult to raise teams. Warrington Grammar School visited Chester but had to bow the knee to the King's School who secured a majority of 21. Collins (25) was the top scorer for the winners, T. A. Sterling (11), being the only Warrington player to reach double figures. Dawson, for Warrington, captured eight wickets for 21 runs. --- Latchford Baptists suffered a reverse at the hands of Highlield Tannery who triumphed by 10 runs. The batting generally was poor, T. Coiling° (13). being the highest scorer. E. F. Cliffa topped the Latchford score list with 10, the chief feature being a great array of " ducks." -- Latchford Baptists 2ad drew with Highfield Tannery 2nd, who made 63 for 4 wickets against the Baptists' 99. W. Harrison made a splendid 29 for tha Tannery and carried out his bat. For Latchford fine displays were forthcoming from Once (27), Bramhall (23) and Downes (25.) --- Marshhouse-lane gains i an easy victory over an eleven captained by Mr. Riley, G. Mann and Mr. Riley each making 17 for their respective sides. Grappanhall failed against Barnton, whe piled on 95 as against Grappenhall's 61. James Powell (22 not out) and T. Kirkham (21) were in fine form for the winners, while W. Wicks and A. Slack each made 19 for Grappen- hall. Bowling. There is not much to record in local bowling circles this week, the works competition having been suspended until next Saturday as the green is wanted for other purposes. Owing to the holidays many bowlers were out of town last week-end. In the club Championship Competition under the auspices of the Lancashire and Cheshire Association, there was a capital game at Withing,ton between Warrington Cemetery and Prest- wich Conservatives. The Warringtonians are to be heartily congratulated on winning by 31 points. T. Ellison, the individual merit champion,was in excellent form and accounted for his opponent (J. Dickenson) by 21-8. G. Ball, senior, lost to J. Slater by 19-21 but G. Ball, junior, defeated 11. Crompton by 21-11. -- Great interest is being shown at the Liberal Club in the competition for the Crostield Challenge Cup presented by the wife of the Member for the Borough. Over one hundred entries have been received, and the first round (which closes on the 21st inst.) is now in 'progress. The green is in capital order, and plenty of good bowling is witnessed every evening at the Liberal headquarters. -- We have previously referred in these notes to the admirable provision which is made for bowlers on Messrs. Rylands' Bros'. workmen's recreation ground. Visitors to the gronnd lately will have noticed that the new large pavilion is nearly roofed in and they will agree that the work reflects great credit on the archi- tect,Mr. S. P. Silcock, P.R.1.8.A., of Warrington. The building is of half timber construction and roofed with red tiles. Remarkable progress has been made since the commencement, at the beginning of April. A large staff of men are at work. The builder is Mr. Prank Warburton of Stockton Heath. -- Cycling. Full advantage was taken of the fine weather that prevailed during the holidays, Hunt Cross being visited on Friday, while on Saturday a fair muster of members were to be found at Bollington, the Faradon week-end having been deferred until to-day, when the members will journey on from Beeston. It was qnite refreshing to find such a good torn-up for the mid-week fixture to Hoo Green on Tuesday evening, nearly a score of members putting in an appearance. -- Very little progress was made with the handicap on Wednesday, the elements being rather unfavourable from a bowler's point of view. -- To-day the Club pay their annual visit to the home of their President, Mr. John Naylor, at Beeston Towers. This event is recognised as the red letter day of the season 70 or 80 members and lady friends generally contriving to put in an appearance. Granted favour- able weather to-day's event promises to be as successful as any of its predecessors. --- Junior Football. There will be a meeting of the Warrington and District Junior Football League on Tuesday next on Orford Albions Club Ground, at Orford-lane, at 7.30. Secretaries or representatives of junior clubs who are interested in the reforming of the League are requested to kindly attend.
